subproblem.statement: Dilation of currents (the change of scale x ↦ ρx used to pass from 5.1 to 5.3). For N ∈ ℕ, ρ > 0 and k ∈ ℕ, writing η_ρ^#ω(x) := ρ^k ω(ρx) (the pull-back of a k-form under x ↦ ρx) and calling (X, Y) a ρ-pair in degree k if Y(ω) = X(η) for all test forms ω, η with η(x) = ρ^k ω(ρx) for all x: (1) for every test k-form ω there is a test k-form η with η(x) = ρ^k ω(ρx) for all x; (2) for every X ∈ D_k(ℝ^N) there is Y with (X, Y) a ρ-pair (Y = (η_ρ)_#X); (3) for every ρ-pair (X, Y) in degree k: M(Y) = ρ^k M(X), spt Y = ρ·spt X, X integer multiplicity ⇒ Y integer multiplicity, and IsLatticeChain 1 β X ⇒ IsLatticeChain ρ β Y for every β : LatticeFaceIndex k N → ℝ; (4) if (X, Y) is a ρ-pair in degree k + 1 then ∂Y(ω) = ∂X(η) for all test k-forms ω, η with η(x) = ρ^k ω(ρx).

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, the printed sentence introducing 5.3 (“obtained from the above by first changing scale x → ρ⁻¹x, then applying 5.1, then changing scale back by x → ρx”), push-forward by a smooth proper map 2.23 and 2.24(1), as detailed in Part D (D1–D2) and A4(e) of the parent proof (“η_{ρ#}[[F]] = [[ρF]]”; masses scale by ρ^k for k-currents; supports scale by ρ; images of integer multiplicity currents under dilations are integer multiplicity).

Notation. Fix N, ρ > 0 and k. For a k-form ω put (η_ρ^#ω)(x) := ρ^k ω(ρx). This is the pull-back of ω by η_ρ(x) := ρx: (η_ρ^#ω)(x)(v₁,…,v_k) = ω(ρx)(ρv₁,…,ρv_k) = ρ^kω(ρx)(v₁,…,v_k). Note η_ρ^#η_{1/ρ}^#ω = ω and η_{1/ρ}^#η_ρ^#ω = ω. Say that (X, Y) is a ρ-pair in degree k if Y(ω) = X(η) whenever ω, η are test forms with η(x) = ρ^kω(ρx) for all x (this is the hypothesis appearing in the statement). Elements of TestFormOn univ k with the same underlying function are equal, so for a ρ-pair Y(ω) = X(η_ρ^#ω) for all ω, once η_ρ^#ω is known to be a test form (Step 1). H^k = μHE[k]. Degenerate dimensions: if k > N every k-covector on ℝ^N vanishes, every test form and every current of degree k is 0, LatticeFaceIndex k N is empty and all conclusions hold trivially (0 is integer multiplicity); k = 0 and N = 0 need no change below.

1. Pull-backs of test forms (first conjunct). Let ω be a test form. x ↦ ρ^kω(ρx) is C^∞ (composition of the smooth ω with the linear map x ↦ ρx, times a constant) and its topological support is ρ⁻¹·tsupport ω (η_ρ is a homeomorphism), a compact set; trivially tsupport ⊆ univ. Hence η := η_ρ^#ω ∈ TestFormOn univ k, with η(x) = ρ^k•ω(ρ•x) for all x.

2. Existence of the push-forward (second conjunct; 2.23). Given X ∈ D_k(ℝ^N), define Y(ω) := X(η_ρ^#ω). Y is linear (η_ρ^# is linear). Continuity: if ω_j → 0 in Simon's test-form topology (supports in a common compact K, all derivatives → 0 uniformly on K), then the η_ρ^#ω_j are supported in the compact set ρ⁻¹K and, by the chain rule, the i-th derivative of η_ρ^#ω_j at x is ρ^{k+i} times the i-th derivative of ω_j at ρx (composed with ρ·id in each slot), so it tends to 0 uniformly; thus η_ρ^#ω_j → 0 in the test-form topology and Y(ω_j) = X(η_ρ^#ω_j) → 0 (continuity of X). So Y ∈ GeometricCurrentOn univ k, and (X, Y) is a ρ-pair by construction.

3. Inverse relation. If (X, Y) is a ρ-pair, then X(ω′) = Y(η_{1/ρ}^#ω′) for all test forms ω′: apply the pair property to ω := η_{1/ρ}^#ω′ (a test form by Step 1) and η := ω′ = η_ρ^#ω.

From now on (X, Y) is a ρ-pair in degree k.

4. Mass (2.23 with |η_ρ^#ω| = ρ^k|ω∘η_ρ|). covectorEuclideanNorm(cα) = |c|·covectorEuclideanNorm(α) (all coefficients α(e_γ) scale by c). If ω is admissible for M(Y) (|ω(x)| ≤ 1 for all x), then ρ^{−k}η_ρ^#ω is admissible for M(X) (|ρ^{−k}η_ρ^#ω(x)| = |ω(ρx)| ≤ 1), so ENNReal.ofReal(Y(ω)) = ENNReal.ofReal(ρ^k X(ρ^{−k}η_ρ^#ω)) ≤ ρ^k M(X); hence M(Y) ≤ ρ^k M(X). By Step 3 and the same argument with ρ replaced by 1/ρ, M(X) ≤ ρ^{−k}M(Y). Therefore Y.mass = ENNReal.ofReal(ρ^k)·X.mass (also when X.mass = ∞, since then M(Y) ≥ ρ^kM(X) = ∞).

5. Support. Let W be open with compact closure. If X vanishes on ρ⁻¹W and tsupport ω ⊆ W, then tsupport η_ρ^#ω = ρ⁻¹tsupport ω ⊆ ρ⁻¹W, so Y(ω) = X(η_ρ^#ω) = 0: Y vanishes on W. Conversely, by Step 3, if Y vanishes on W then X vanishes on ρ⁻¹W. Since W ↦ ρ⁻¹W is a bijection of the open sets with compact closure (closure(ρ⁻¹W) = ρ⁻¹closure(W)), zeroRegion(Y) = ρ·zeroRegion(X), and Y.support = univ ∖ zeroRegion(Y) = ρ·(univ ∖ zeroRegion(X)) = (fun x => ρ • x) '' X.support.

6. Dilation of Hausdorff measure. For every s ≥ 0 and E ⊆ ℝ^N, H^s(ρE) = ρ^sH^s(E) (coverings scale: diam(ρA) = ρ·diam A; the normalizing constant of μHE[s] is a fixed factor). Consequently, for E H^k-measurable and g integrable on ρE: ∫_{ρE} g dH^k = ρ^k∫_E g(ρx) dH^k(x); and η_ρ, η_{1/ρ} map H^k-null sets to H^k-null sets.

7. Integer multiplicity (parent A4(e)). Let X = τ(M, θ, ξ) with IsRectifiableTriple univ k M θ ξ and θ natural-valued on M. Put M′ := ρM, θ′(y) := θ(ρ⁻¹y), ξ′(y) := ξ(ρ⁻¹y). For every test form ω, by linearity of ξ(x) and Step 6 with g(y) := θ′(y)ξ′(y)(ω(y)):
 Y(ω) = X(η_ρ^#ω) = ∫_M θ(x)ξ(x)(ρ^kω(ρx))dH^k(x) = ρ^k∫_M θ(x)ξ(x)(ω(ρx))dH^k(x) = ρ^kρ^{−k}∫_{ρM} θ′(y)ξ′(y)(ω(y))dH^k(y) = tauAction k M′ θ′ ξ′ ω.
 Triple conditions for (M′, θ′, ξ′): M′ ⊆ univ; M′ is H^k-null-measurable (image of a null-measurable set under the homeomorphism η_ρ, which preserves Borel sets and null sets by Step 6); countably k-rectifiable: if M ⊆ M₀ ∪ ⋃_jF_j(ℝ^k) with H^k(M₀) = 0 and F_j Lipschitz, then M′ ⊆ ρM₀ ∪ ⋃_j(ρF_j)(ℝ^k) with H^k(ρM₀) = 0 and ρF_j Lipschitz; θ′ > 0 and natural-valued on M′; for compact K, ∫_{M′∩K}θ′dH^k = ρ^k∫_{M∩ρ⁻¹K}θdH^k < ∞ (ρ⁻¹K compact), so θ′ is integrable on M′ ∩ K; ξ′ is a.e. strongly measurable for H^k⌞M′ (ξ′ = ξ∘η_{1/ρ} and η_{1/ρ} maps H^k⌞M′-null sets to H^k⌞M-null sets). Orientation: let x ∈ M be a point where ξ(x) = ±simpleNVector τ for an orthonormal τ with HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt k M θ x (span τ), and y := ρx ∈ M′. For r > 0, blowUpMap y r '' M′ = {r⁻¹(ρz − ρx) : z ∈ M} = blowUpMap x (r/ρ) '' M, and θ′(y + rw) = θ(x + (r/ρ)w). Hence for f ∈ C_c(ℝ^N):
 ∫_{blowUpMap y r '' M′} f(w)θ′(y + rw)dH^k(w) = ∫_{blowUpMap x (r/ρ) '' M} f(w)θ(x + (r/ρ)w)dH^k(w) → θ(x)∫_{span τ}f dH^k = θ′(y)∫_{span τ}f dH^k
 as r ↓ 0 (because r/ρ ↓ 0); so HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt k M′ θ′ y (span τ) and ξ′(y) = ξ(x) = ±simpleNVector τ. The exceptional set in M′ is the image under η_ρ of an H^k-null subset of M, hence H^k-null (Step 6). So IsIntegerMultiplicity Y.

8. Lattice chains (parent D2: η_{ρ#}[[F]] = [[ρF]]). For F = (z, α) ∈ LatticeFaceIndex k N, latticeFace ρ F = ρ·latticeFace 1 F (the defining conditions ρz_i ≤ x_i ≤ ρ(z_i + 1) for i ∈ range α and x_i = ρz_i otherwise are those of latticeFace 1 F for ρ⁻¹x). By Step 6, for every test form ω:
 latticeFaceAction 1 F (η_ρ^#ω) = ∫_{latticeFace 1 F} ρ^kω(ρx)(e_{α₁},…,e_{α_k})dH^k(x) = ∫_{latticeFace ρ F} ω(y)(e_{α₁},…,e_{α_k})dH^k(y) = latticeFaceAction ρ F ω.
 Hence, if IsLatticeChain 1 β X, then for every ω: Y(ω) = X(η_ρ^#ω) = ∑'_F β_F·latticeFaceAction 1 F (η_ρ^#ω) = ∑'_F β_F·latticeFaceAction ρ F ω (the two families of summands are equal term by term, so their tsums are equal), i.e. IsLatticeChain ρ β Y.

9. Boundary (fourth conjunct; 2.24(1)). Let (X, Y) be a ρ-pair in degree k + 1 and let ω, η be test k-forms with η(x) = ρ^kω(ρx). Pull-back commutes with d: with η = η_ρ^#ω, Dη(x)(v) = ρ^{k+1}(Dω)(ρx)(v) and dη(x)(v₀,…,v_k) = Σ_i(−1)^iDη(x)(v_i)(v₀,…,v̂_i,…,v_k) = ρ^{k+1}(dω)(ρx)(v₀,…,v_k), i.e. the test form exteriorDerivativeTestOn univ k η equals η_ρ^#(exteriorDerivativeTestOn univ k ω) in degree k + 1. Therefore Y.boundary ω = Y(dω) = X(η_ρ^#dω) = X(dη) = X.boundary η.

10. Conclusion. Steps 1, 2 give the first two conjuncts; Steps 4, 5, 7, 8 give, for every ρ-pair (X, Y) in degree k, Y.mass = ENNReal.ofReal(ρ^k)·X.mass, Y.support = (fun x => ρ • x) '' X.support, IsIntegerMultiplicity X → IsIntegerMultiplicity Y and IsLatticeChain 1 β X → IsLatticeChain ρ β Y for every β; Step 9 gives the boundary conjunct. ∎

Inverse relation via η_{1/ρ}; mass scaling M(Y) = ρ^kM(X); support scaling spt Y = ρ spt X.
Hausdorff measure scaling H^k(ρE) = ρ^kH^k(E); Y = τ(ρM, θ(·/ρ), ξ(·/ρ)) with blow-ups η_{ρx,r}(ρM) = η_{x,r/ρ}(M): integrality preserved.
latticeFace ρ F = ρ·latticeFace 1 F, so latticeFaceAction 1 F (η_ρ^#ω) = latticeFaceAction ρ F ω and lattice chains map to lattice chains.
d commutes with η_ρ^#, giving the boundary relation.

subproblem.title: Choice of a good centre a for two finite measures (5.1, printed (1)–(7))
subproblem.statement: Choice of a good centre (printed (1)–(7) of the proof of 5.1). Let m, ℓ ∈ ℕ with ℓ ≥ 1, n := m + 1, d := n + ℓ. There is c = c(m,ℓ) ∈ [0,∞) such that for any two finite Borel measures μ₁, μ₂ on ℝ^d there is a ∈ ℝ^d with Σ_i(a_i − 1/2)² < 1/16 such that, for La := L_{ℓ−1}(a) = {y : ∃ J, |J| = m + 2, y_i − a_i ∈ ℤ ∀ i ∈ J}, every σ ∈ (0, 1/4) and i ∈ {1, 2}: μ_i({x : dist(x, La) < σ}) ≤ c·σ^{m+2}·μ_i(ℝ^d).

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, §5, printed “Proof of the Deformation Theorem”, displays (1)–(7) (pp. 163–164), as reproduced in steps C1–C2 of the parent proof, with the measures M(T⌞·) and M(∂T⌞·) replaced by two arbitrary finite Borel measures μ₁, μ₂ (in the deformation argument they are the mass measures μ_T, μ_∂T, for which M(T⌞A) = μ_T(A)). Errata applied: book k = ℓ; (vi) the printed measure estimate (5) is replaced by the Fubini bound of Step 4 (the printed constants are not needed).

Notation. n := m + 1, d := n + ℓ, ℝ^d = Eucl(m+1+ℓ), C := [0,1]^d, q := (1/2,…,1/2), ω_k := L^k(B_1(0)) for k ≥ 1 and ω₀ := 1. For J ⊆ {1,…,d} with |J| = n + 1 = m + 2 (there are N := C(d, n+1) ≥ 1 such J because ℓ ≥ 1) let S_J := span{e_i : i ∈ J}, p_J : ℝ^d → S_J the orthogonal projection (keep the coordinates in J), x_J := p_J(q), and let B_r(g) denote open balls in S_J (dimension n + 1). 3. Size of the bad set (printed (2)–(4)). For b ∈ B_J choose σ_b ∈ (0,1/4) with μ(V_J(b,σ_b)) > βσ_b^{n+1}μ(ℝ^d).  L^d(A_J) ≤ L^{n+1}(B_J)·ω_{ℓ−1}4^{1−ℓ} ≤ 5^{n+1}ω_{n+1}ω_{ℓ−1}4^{1−ℓ}β⁻¹.

Let La = L(a). For σ ∈ (0, 1/4) and i ∈ {1,2}, by (1.1) and the definition of G_J^{(i)}:
 μ_i({x : dist(x, La) < σ}) ≤ Σ_J μ_i(V_J(p_J(a), σ)) ≤ Nβσ^{n+1}μ_i(ℝ^d) = Nβσ^{m+2}μ_i(univ).

6. Conclusion. c := Nβ ∈ [0,∞) depends only on (m, ℓ), and the point a of Step 5 has all required properties, for any finite Borel measures μ₁, μ₂. ∎

subproblem.title: Integer combinations of integer multiplicity currents (Simon 3.2(1))
subproblem.statement: Integer combinations of integer multiplicity currents (Simon 3.2(1)). For N, k ∈ ℕ, integer multiplicity X, Y ∈ D_k(ℝ^N), integers a, b and Z ∈ D_k(ℝ^N) with Z(ω) = a·X(ω) + b·Y(ω) for every test form ω, Z is integer multiplicity.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N k : ℕ) (X Y Z : GeometricCurrentOn (univ : Set (Eucl N)) k) (a b : ℤ), IsIntegerMultiplicity X → IsIntegerMultiplicity Y → (∀ ω, Z ω = a * X ω + b * Y ω) → IsIntegerMultiplicity Z
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, Remark 3.2(1) (p. 146: “If T₁, T₂ ∈ D_n(U) are integer multiplicity, then so is p₁T₁ + p₂T₂, p₁, p₂ ∈ ℤ”), printed without proof; the argument is A4(c) of the parent proof (“on M₁∩M₂ the approximate tangent spaces agree a.e., ξ₂ = ±ξ₁, and τ(M₁,θ₁,ξ₁) + τ(M₂,θ₂,ξ₂) = τ(M,θ,ξ) with θ = |θ₁ ± θ₂| on M₁∩M₂, points with θ = 0 removed, θ = θ_i on M_i∖M_{3−i}; negatives flip ξ”), with the tangent-space facts supplied from Simon Ch. 3, 1.4–1.9 (in particular Remark 1.8(1)) and the Upper Density Theorem Ch. 1, 3.6.

Setting. H^k = μHE[k], U = ℝ^N (univ). X = τ(M₁, θ₁, ξ₁), Y = τ(M₂, θ₂, ξ₂) with IsRectifiableTriple univ k M_i θ_i ξ_i and θ_i(x) ∈ {1,2,…} for x ∈ M_i; a, b ∈ ℤ; Z(ω) = aX(ω) + bY(ω) for all test forms ω. Conventions: for a k-vector w, w^γ := w(dx^γ) (γ increasing), |w| := (Σ_γ(w^γ)²)^{1/2}; for a k-covector α, |α| = covectorEuclideanNorm α; every covector is α = Σ_γα(e_γ)dx^γ, so |w(α)| ≤ |α||w|. Unit fact: if τ₁,…,τ_k are orthonormal then |simpleNVector τ| = 1, because its coordinates (simpleNVector τ)^γ = det(τ_i·e_{γ_j}) are the k×k minors of the matrix with columns τ₁,…,τ_k and, by the Cauchy–Binet formula, Σ_γ det(τ_i·e_{γ_j})² = det(τ_i·τ_j) = 1; consequently, whenever IsRectifiableTriple U k M θ ξ holds, |ξ| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M (orientation clause). Hence |ξ_i| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M_i. Degenerate dimensions: if k > N, every k-covector on ℝ^N is 0, so Z = 0 = τ(∅, 0, 0) is integer multiplicity; for k = 0 the frames τ are empty, span τ = {0}, simpleNVector of the empty family is evaluation at the empty tuple, and the argument below applies verbatim; N = 0 needs no change. Since θ_i ≥ 1 on M_i and θ_i is integrable on M_i ∩ K for compact K, H^k(M_i ∩ K) ≤ ∫_{M_i∩K}θ_i < ∞: the measures H^k⌞M₁, H^k⌞M₂ and H^k⌞(M₁ ∪ M₂) are locally finite. For f ∈ C_c(ℝ^N), x ∈ ℝ^N, r > 0, η_{x,r}(y) := r⁻¹(y − x) is a similarity of ratio 1/r, so ∫_{η_{x,r}(E)} g dH^k = r^{−k}∫_E g∘η_{x,r} dH^k, and x + r·η_{x,r}(z) = z. Say that a set E has (unweighted) approximate tangent space Π at x (Simon Ch. 3, 1.4) if finrank Π = k and ∫_{η_{x,r}(E)} f dH^k → ∫_Π f dH^k as r ↓ 0 for every f ∈ C_c(ℝ^N); HasWATS(E, θ, x, Π) abbreviates HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt k E θ x Π (Ch. 3, 1.7).

1. Lemma 1 (locality). Let E ⊆ E′ be H^k-null-measurable with H^k⌞E′ locally finite, and let θ be positive on E′ and integrable on E′ ∩ K for compact K. Then for H^k-a.e. x ∈ E and every Π: E has approximate tangent space Π at x ⟺ E′ does; and HasWATS(E, θ, x, Π) ⟺ HasWATS(E′, θ, x, Π).
 Proof. By the Upper Density Theorem (Simon Ch. 1, 3.6, with Remark 3.7(2)) applied to the locally finite measures H^k⌞E′ and θH^k⌞E′ and their subset E′ ∖ E, for H^k-a.e. x ∉ E′ ∖ E (in particular a.e. x ∈ E) both H^k((E′∖E) ∩ B_ρ(x))/ρ^k and (θH^k)((E′∖E) ∩ B_ρ(x))/ρ^k tend to 0 as ρ ↓ 0. For such x, f with spt f ⊆ B_R(0) and r > 0: |∫_{η_{x,r}(E′)} f − ∫_{η_{x,r}(E)} f| = |∫_{η_{x,r}(E′∖E)} f| ≤ ‖f‖r^{−k}H^k((E′∖E) ∩ B_{Rr}(x)) → 0, and likewise |∫_{η_{x,r}(E′∖E)} f(y)θ(x + ry)dH^k(y)| ≤ ‖f‖r^{−k}(θH^k)((E′∖E) ∩ B_{Rr}(x)) → 0 (η_{x,r} is injective). Hence the defining limits coincide.

2. Lemma 2 (weights; Simon Ch. 3, Remark 1.8(1)). Let E be H^k-null-measurable with H^k⌞E locally finite and θ positive, H^k-measurable on E and integrable on E ∩ K for compact K. Then for H^k-a.e. x ∈ E and every Π: HasWATS(E, θ, x, Π) ⟺ E has approximate tangent space Π at x.
 Proof. By Lusin's theorem (Simon Ch. 1, 1.17) applied to θ on the finite-measure sets E ∩ B_j(0), there are compact sets K₁ ⊆ K₂ ⊆ ⋯ ⊆ E with H^k(E ∖ ⋃_jK_j) = 0 and θ|_{K_j} continuous. As in Lemma 1, for each j there is an H^k-null set Z_j such that for x ∈ K_j ∖ Z_j both H^k⌞(E∖K_j) and θH^k⌞(E∖K_j) have k-density 0 at x. Fix j, x ∈ K_j ∖ Z_j, f ∈ C_c with spt f ⊆ B_R(0) and put I(r) := ∫_{η_{x,r}(K_j)} f dH^k, I_θ(r) := ∫_{η_{x,r}(K_j)} f(y)θ(x + ry)dH^k(y). Then ∫_{η_{x,r}(E)} f = I(r) + o(1) and ∫_{η_{x,r}(E)} f(y)θ(x + ry)dH^k(y) = I_θ(r) + o(1) as r ↓ 0. With ε(r) := sup{|θ(z) − θ(x)| : z ∈ K_j ∩ B_{Rr}(x)} → 0 (continuity of θ|_{K_j} at x), |I_θ(r) − θ(x)I(r)| ≤ ε(r)‖f‖r^{−k}H^k(K_j ∩ B_{Rr}(x)). (⇐) If E has approximate tangent space Π at x, testing the definition with a continuous f₁ ≥ 1_{B_R(0)} shows that r^{−k}H^k(E ∩ B_{Rr}(x)) stays bounded as r ↓ 0, so I_θ(r) − θ(x)I(r) → 0 and ∫_{η_{x,r}(E)} f(y)θ(x + ry) → θ(x)∫_Π f: HasWATS(E, θ, x, Π). (⇒) If HasWATS(E, θ, x, Π), the same test shows that r^{−k}∫_{E∩B_{Rr}(x)}θ dH^k is bounded; since θ ≥ θ(x)/2 > 0 on K_j ∩ B_{Rr}(x) for small r, r^{−k}H^k(K_j ∩ B_{Rr}(x)) is bounded, hence again I_θ(r) − θ(x)I(r) → 0, θ(x)I(r) → θ(x)∫_Π f, and (θ(x) > 0) ∫_{η_{x,r}(E)} f → ∫_Π f. As E ∖ ⋃_j(K_j ∖ Z_j) is H^k-null, the lemma follows.

3. Corollary 3 (tangent spaces agree on the overlap). For H^k-a.e. x ∈ M₁ ∩ M₂: if HasWATS(M₁, θ₁, x, Π₁) and HasWATS(M₂, θ₂, x, Π₂), then Π₁ = Π₂.
 Proof. Outside an H^k-null set, Lemma 2 (for (M₁, θ₁) and (M₂, θ₂)) and Lemma 1 (for M₁ ∩ M₂ ⊆ M₁ and M₁ ∩ M₂ ⊆ M₂) show that M₁ ∩ M₂ has approximate tangent spaces Π₁ and Π₂ at x. Then ∫_{Π₁}f dH^k = ∫_{Π₂}f dH^k for all f ∈ C_c, so H^k⌞Π₁ = H^k⌞Π₂ (both are locally finite Borel measures, hence determined by their integrals of C_c functions), and taking supports, Π₁ = Π₂ (as in SimonGMT's proof of HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt.unique).

4. Orientations on the overlap. Let Γ_i ⊆ M_i be the set where the orientation clause of the i-th triple holds: ξ_i(x) = ±simpleNVector τ^i(x) with τ^i(x) orthonormal and HasWATS(M_i, θ_i, x, span τ^i(x)); H^k(M_i ∖ Γ_i) = 0. By Corollary 3, for H^k-a.e. x ∈ M₁ ∩ M₂, span τ¹(x) = span τ²(x) =: Π. Two orthonormal bases of the k-dimensional space Π are related by an orthogonal matrix O (τ²_i = Σ_j O_{ij}τ¹_j), and by multilinearity and alternation of covectors, simpleNVector τ² = det(O)·simpleNVector τ¹ with det O = ±1. Hence ξ₂(x) = ±ξ₁(x) for H^k-a.e. x ∈ M₁ ∩ M₂ (for k = 0 both are ± the same 0-vector).

5. The new triple. On M₁ ∩ M₂ let ε(x) := 1 if ξ₂(x) = ξ₁(x) and ε(x) := −1 otherwise; ε is H^k-measurable on M₁ ∩ M₂ (ξ₁, ξ₂ are a.e. strongly measurable there), and ξ₂ = εξ₁ H^k-a.e. on M₁ ∩ M₂ by Step 4. Define s : M₁ ∪ M₂ → ℤ by s := aθ₁ + εbθ₂ on M₁ ∩ M₂, s := aθ₁ on M₁ ∖ M₂, s := bθ₂ on M₂ ∖ M₁, and
 M := {x ∈ M₁ ∪ M₂ : s(x) ≠ 0}, θ := |s|, ξ := sign(s)ξ₁ on M ∩ M₁, ξ := sign(s)ξ₂ on M ∖ M₁ (ξ := 0 off M).
 Then θ(x) ∈ {1,2,…} for every x ∈ M, and the k-vector field κ := aθ₁ξ₁1_{M₁} + bθ₂ξ₂1_{M₂} satisfies κ = sξ₁ H^k-a.e. on M₁ and κ = sξ₂ on M₂ ∖ M₁, i.e. κ = θξ1_M H^k-a.e. on M₁ ∪ M₂.

6. Z = τ(M, θ, ξ). For every test form ω the integrands below are integrable (|ξ_i(ω)| ≤ ‖ω‖ a.e., θ_i integrable on M_i ∩ tsupport ω, θ ≤ |a|θ₁1_{M₁} + |b|θ₂1_{M₂}), and
 Z(ω) = a∫_{M₁}θ₁ξ₁(ω)dH^k + b∫_{M₂}θ₂ξ₂(ω)dH^k = ∫_{M₁∪M₂}κ(ω)dH^k = ∫_Mθξ(ω)dH^k = tauAction k M θ ξ ω.

7. Triple conditions. M ⊆ univ. M is H^k-null-measurable: s is H^k-measurable on the null-measurable set M₁ ∪ M₂, so {s ≠ 0} is null-measurable. M ⊆ M₁ ∪ M₂ is countably k-rectifiable (union of two countably k-rectifiable sets, then mono). θ > 0 on M. θ ≤ |a|θ₁1_{M₁} + |b|θ₂1_{M₂} is integrable on M ∩ K for compact K. ξ is a.e. strongly measurable for H^k⌞M (built from ξ₁, ξ₂, sign(s) and measurable sets). Orientation: H^k⌞M is locally finite (M ⊆ M₁ ∪ M₂). For H^k-a.e. x ∈ M ∩ M₁ we have x ∈ Γ₁, ξ(x) = ±ξ₁(x) = ±simpleNVector τ¹(x), and, applying successively (each step outside an H^k-null set) Lemma 2 to (M₁, θ₁), Lemma 1 to M ∩ M₁ ⊆ M₁, Lemma 1 to M ∩ M₁ ⊆ M (with H^k⌞M locally finite), and Lemma 2 to (M, θ): HasWATS(M₁, θ₁, x, span τ¹(x)) ⇒ M₁ has approximate tangent space span τ¹(x) at x ⇒ M ∩ M₁ has it ⇒ M has it ⇒ HasWATS(M, θ, x, span τ¹(x)). subproblem.statement: Completeness of integer multiplicity currents (Simon 3.13). For N, k ∈ ℕ, let T ∈ D_k(ℝ^N) and let T_j ∈ D_k(ℝ^N) (j ∈ ℕ) be integer multiplicity currents such that for every ε > 0 there is J with M(D) < ε for every j ≥ J and every current D with D(ω) = T(ω) − T_j(ω) for all test forms ω (i.e. M(T − T_j) → 0). Then T is integer multiplicity.

Below the printed proof is written out with the details it leaves to the reader: the lower bound (1) for the mass of a difference, the passage to an a.e. convergent subsequence, and the identification of the approximate tangent spaces (Simon Ch. 3, 1.4–1.9, Remark 1.8(1), and the Upper Density Theorem Ch. 1, 3.6).

T ∈ D_k(ℝ^N), T_j = τ(M_j, θ_j, ξ_j) with IsRectifiableTriple univ k M_j θ_j ξ_j and θ_j natural-valued on M_j, and (hypothesis) for every ε > 0 there is J such that M(D) < ε for every j ≥ J and every current D with D(ω) = T(ω) − T_j(ω) for all ω. Extend θ_j := 0 and ξ_j := 0 off M_j and put κ_j := θ_jξ_j. Then M(Y) ≥ ∫|κ|dλ′ (in [0,∞]). Proof: fix R > 0 and ε > 0, let ν := |κ|λ′⌞B_R(0) (a finite Borel measure) and u := κ/|κ| on {κ ≠ 0}. Let u♭ := Σ_γu^γdx^γ (|u♭| = 1 and ⟨u♭, u⟩ = 1 on K′), extend u♭|_{K′} continuously to ℝ^N (Tietze), compose with y ↦ y/max{1,|y|} and multiply by a continuous χ with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 on K′ and compact support in B_R(0): this gives f ∈ C_c with |f| ≤ 1, spt f ⊆ B_R(0) and ∫⟨f, κ⟩dλ′ ≥ ν(K′) − ν(ℝ^N ∖ K′) ≥ ν(ℝ^N) − 4ε (|⟨α, w⟩| ≤ |α||w|). The mollifications f_δ are test forms with |f_δ| ≤ 1, supported in a fixed compact set and converging uniformly to f, so Y(f_δ) → ∫⟨f, κ⟩dλ′ by dominated convergence and M(Y) ≥ ∫_{B_R(0)}|κ|dλ′ − 4ε. Let ε ↓ 0 and R ↑ ∞.
 Applied to Y := T_i − T_j, λ′ := H^k⌞(M_i ∪ M_j) (locally finite) and κ := κ_i − κ_j (integrable on bounded sets, since θ_i, θ_j are), and noting that κ_i, κ_j vanish off M_i ∪ M_j: (1) ∫|κ_i − κ_j|dλ ≤ M(T_i − T_j).

3. Convergence of the densities (printed (2), (3)). By (1) and Step 1, Σ_j∫|κ_{j+1} − κ_j|dλ < ∞; since ||κ_{j+1}| − |κ_j|| ≤ |κ_{j+1} − κ_j| and |κ_j| = θ_j λ-a.e., also Σ_j∫|θ_{j+1} − θ_j|dλ < ∞. 5. Approximate tangent spaces (Simon Ch. 3, 1.4–1.9). Say a set E has approximate tangent space Π at x if finrank Π = k and ∫_{η_{x,r}(E)}f dH^k → ∫_Πf dH^k (r ↓ 0) for all f ∈ C_c(ℝ^N), where η_{x,r}(y) := r⁻¹(y − x) is a similarity of ratio 1/r (∫_{η_{x,r}(E)}g dH^k = r^{−k}∫_Eg∘η_{x,r}dH^k, x + r·η_{x,r}(z) = z); HasWATS(E, ϑ, x, Π) abbreviates HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt k E ϑ x Π.
 Lemma A (locality). If E ⊆ E′ are H^k-null-measurable, H^k⌞E′ is locally finite and ϑ is positive and locally integrable on E′, then for H^k-a.e. x ∈ E and every Π: E has approximate tangent space Π at x ⟺ E′ has; and HasWATS(E, ϑ, x, Π) ⟺ HasWATS(E′, ϑ, x, Π). Proof: by the Upper Density Theorem (Simon Ch. 1, 3.6 with Remark 3.7(2)), H^k⌞(E′∖E) and ϑH^k⌞(E′∖E) have k-density 0 at H^k-a.e. x ∉ E′ ∖ E; for such x and spt f ⊆ B_R(0), |∫_{η_{x,r}(E′∖E)}f| ≤ ‖f‖r^{−k}H^k((E′∖E) ∩ B_{Rr}(x)) → 0 and |∫_{η_{x,r}(E′∖E)}f(y)ϑ(x+ry)dH^k(y)| ≤ ‖f‖r^{−k}(ϑH^k)((E′∖E) ∩ B_{Rr}(x)) → 0.
 Lemma B (weights; Ch. 3, Remark 1.8(1)). If E is H^k-null-measurable with H^k⌞E locally finite and ϑ is positive, measurable and locally integrable on E, then for H^k-a.e. x ∈ E and every Π: HasWATS(E, ϑ, x, Π) ⟺ E has approximate tangent space Π at x. Proof: Lusin gives compact K₁ ⊆ K₂ ⊆ ⋯ ⊆ E with H^k(E ∖ ⋃K_i) = 0 and ϑ|_{K_i} continuous; at H^k-a.e. x ∈ K_i, H^k⌞(E∖K_i) and ϑH^k⌞(E∖K_i) have density 0 (as in Lemma A), so both defining integrals can be computed on η_{x,r}(K_i) up to o(1); on K_i ∩ B_{Rr}(x), |ϑ − ϑ(x)| ≤ ε(r) → 0, which makes the weighted integral equal to ϑ(x) times the unweighted one up to ε(r)‖f‖r^{−k}H^k(K_i ∩ B_{Rr}(x)); this quantity is bounded under either hypothesis (test with a continuous f ≥ 1_{B_R(0)}; under the weighted hypothesis use ϑ ≥ ϑ(x)/2 > 0 on K_i ∩ B_{Rr}(x) for small r), and ϑ(x) > 0; hence the two limits correspond.

M₊ ⊆ univ; M₊ ⊆ M_∞ is countably k-rectifiable and H^k-null-measurable (θ is λ-measurable); θ is natural-valued and positive on M₊; for compact K, ∫_{M₊∩K}θ ≤ ∫_Kθ₁dλ + Σ_j∫|θ_{j+1} − θ_j|dλ < ∞, so θ is integrable on M₊ ∩ K and H^k⌞M₊ is locally finite (θ ≥ 1 on M₊); ξ is a.e. strongly measurable for H^k⌞M₊ (an a.e. limit of the measurable ξ_j = κ_j/θ_j, see below). For j ≥ j(x), ξ_j(x) = ±simpleNVector τ^j with τ^j orthonormal and HasWATS(M_j, θ_j, x, span τ^j); by Lemma B, Lemma A (twice) and Lemma B again, HasWATS(M₊, θ, x, span τ^j). As θ(x) ≠ 0, the weighted approximate tangent space of (M₊, θ) at x is unique (SimonGMT HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt.unique), so Π := span τ^j does not depend on j ≥ j(x). Let P, Q, k ∈ ℕ, X ∈ D_k(ℝ^P) with X(ω) = tauAction k M θ ξ ω for all ω, where IsRectifiableTriple univ k M θ ξ and θ is natural-valued on M, and let g : ℝ^P → ℝ^Q be Λ-Lipschitz with g⁻¹(K) ∩ spt X compact for every compact K. Then there is an integer multiplicity S ∈ D_k(ℝ^Q) with IsLipschitzPushforward X g S such that, for every sequence (g_j) of C¹ maps ℝ^P → ℝ^Q that are Λ′-Lipschitz for a common Λ′ and converge uniformly to g, and every test form ω on ℝ^Q, ∫_M θ(x)·⟨ω(g_j(x)), Dg_j(x)_#ξ(x)⟩ dH^k(x) → S(ω) (the integrand written as θ x * nVectorPushforward k (fderiv ℝ (gj j) x) (ξ x) (ω (gj j x))).

Source: the consistency step behind Simon's printed remark “Q, R₁ are integer multiplicity by (19), 4.4, 4.5 and 3.13” in the proof of the Deformation Theorem (Ch. 6, §5, p. 166), i.e. A3 of the parent proof (parts (I) and (II)), copied below with the mollified maps g_ε = ϕ_ε * g of the parent replaced by an arbitrary sequence (g_j) of C¹ maps with a common Lipschitz bound converging uniformly to g (the argument of (I) uses only these properties of g_ε). The tools are Simon Ch. 3, §§1–2 (approximate tangent spaces, tangential differential d^Mg, C¹ decomposition of rectifiable sets, Lemma 1.2, Remarks 1.3, 1.5, 1.8), Ch. 2, 3.4 (area formula for injective C¹ maps), Ch. 1, 3.6 (Upper Density Theorem) and Lemma 3.9 of Ch. 6 in the form of the premise LipschitzPushforwardIntegerMultiplicity.

Setting. Write D := P, D′ := Q, H^k = μHE[k]. Assume the premise LipschitzPushforwardIntegerMultiplicity. Let X ∈ D_k(ℝ^D) (GeometricCurrentOn univ k), (M, θ, ξ) with IsRectifiableTriple univ k M θ ξ, θ(x) ∈ ℕ for x ∈ M (hence θ ≥ 1 on M, as θ > 0), and X(ω) = tauAction k M θ ξ ω for all ω, so X = τ(M,θ,ξ) is integer multiplicity. Let g : ℝ^D → ℝ^{D′} be Λ-Lipschitz with g⁻¹(K) ∩ spt X compact for every compact K. For the definition of S below let L(x) := d^Mg_x∘π_{T_xM}, where T_xM is the weighted approximate tangent space of (M,θ) at x and d^Mg_x the tangential differential of Simon Ch. 3, §2 (both defined H^k-a.e. on M; ‖L(x)‖ ≤ Λ), and S(ω) := ∫_Mθ⟨ω(g(x)), L(x)_#ξ(x)⟩dH^k for ω ∈ D^k(ℝ^{D′}). Let (g_j) be any sequence with g_j C¹, Λ′-Lipschitz, and g_j → g uniformly on ℝ^D, and F_j(x) := θ(x)⟨ω(g_j(x)), Dg_j(x)_#ξ(x)⟩ the integrand of the statement. We prove: (I) for every ω, ∫_MF_j dH^k → S(ω); (II) S(ω) = S̃(ω) for all ω, where S̃ is an integer multiplicity current with IsLipschitzPushforward X g S̃ supplied by the premise. Then S̃ is the current required by the statement. Degenerate dimensions: if k > D then μHE[k] = 0 on ℝ^D, X = 0 and every integral vanishes; if k > D′ every k-covector on ℝ^{D′} vanishes, so ω = 0; in both cases (I) and (II) hold trivially (all quantities are 0); for k = 0 see the end of (g); D = 0 or D′ = 0 need no change.

Conventions (stated here so that this proof is self-contained). For an ambient dimension D, e₁,…,e_D is the standard basis of ℝ^D, I(k,D) the set of strictly increasing multi-indices γ = (γ₁ < ⋯ < γ_k) in {1,…,D}, e_γ := (e_{γ₁},…,e_{γ_k}) and dx^γ := dx^{γ₁}∧⋯∧dx^{γ_k}. For a k-covector α (`Covector (Eucl D) k`), |α| := (Σ_γ α(e_γ)²)^{1/2} (`covectorEuclideanNorm`); for a k-form ω, ‖ω‖ := sup_x |ω(x)|; for a k-vector w (`NVector (Eucl D) k`, a linear functional on k-covectors), ⟨α, w⟩ := w(α), w^γ := w(dx^γ) and |w| := (Σ_γ (w^γ)²)^{1/2}; ‖A‖ is the operator norm of a linear map A. Coordinate fact: every k-covector satisfies α = Σ_γ α(e_γ)dx^γ (an alternating k-linear map is determined by its values on increasing tuples of basis vectors, and dx^γ(e_δ) = δ_{γδ}); hence w(α) = Σ_γ α(e_γ)w^γ and |w(α)| ≤ |α|·|w| (Cauchy–Schwarz). Push-forward of k-vectors: for a linear map A : ℝ^D → ℝ^{D′}, A_# = Λ_kA := `nVectorPushforward k A` is characterized by ⟨α, A_#w⟩ = ⟨A^#α, w⟩ with A^#α := α(A·,…,A·) (Simon 1.8–1.9); it is linear and A_#(simpleNVector τ) = simpleNVector(Aτ₁,…,Aτ_k) (Simon 1.10; SimonGMT `nVectorPushforward_simple`). Unit fact: if τ₁,…,τ_k ∈ ℝ^D are orthonormal then |simpleNVector τ| = 1, because its coordinates (simpleNVector τ)^γ = det(τ_i·e_{γ_j}) are the k×k minors of the D×k matrix with columns τ₁,…,τ_k and, by the Cauchy–Binet formula, Σ_γ det(τ_i·e_{γ_j})² = det(τ_i·τ_j) = 1; consequently, whenever `IsRectifiableTriple U k M θ ξ` holds, |ξ| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M (orientation clause). Mass M = `mass`, spt = `support`. Norm of push-forwards: |Λ_kA w| ≤ ‖A‖^k|w| for a linear map A and a k-vector w (the singular values of Λ_kA are products of k singular values of A); hence |⟨α, A_#w⟩| ≤ |α|‖A‖^k|w|.

Proof of (I): ∫_M F_j dH^k → S(ω). Fix ω ∈ D^k(ℝ^{D′}) and the sequence (g_j); put δ_j := sup_x |g_j(x) − g(x)| (→ 0 by uniform convergence) and Λ″ := max{Λ, Λ′}.
 (a) (A fixed compact target neighbourhood.) Let K₀ := tsupport ω and K := {y : dist(y, K₀) ≤ 1}, a compact set. Choose j₀ with δ_j ≤ 1 for j ≥ j₀; g_j is C¹ and Λ′-Lipschitz, so ‖Dg_j‖ ≤ Λ′ everywhere. For j ≥ j₀ we have: g_j(x) ∈ K₀ ⇒ g(x) ∈ K. Hence for all such j, ω(g_j(x)) = 0 unless x ∈ g⁻¹(K), and likewise ω(g(x)) = 0 unless x ∈ g⁻¹(K).
 (b) (The contributing source points lie in one compact set.) K″ := g⁻¹(K) ∩ spt X is compact (properness of g|spt X). Moreover H^k(M ∖ spt X) = 0: X(φ) = 0 for every test form φ supported in the open set ℝ^D ∖ spt X (tsupport φ is a compact subset of the zero region, so it is covered by finitely many relatively compact open sets on which X vanishes, and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to them splits φ into forms annihilated by X); hence, for every γ ∈ I(k,D) and every ball B_R(0), the finite signed measures B ↦ ∫_{B∩M}θξ^γ dH^k on the Borel subsets of the open set B_R(0) ∖ spt X vanish on C_c^∞ functions (test forms φdx^γ), therefore on C_c functions (mollification and dominated convergence), on compact sets (decreasing continuous approximations) and on all Borel sets (Dynkin's π–λ theorem); so θξ = 0 H^k-a.e. on M ∖ spt X, and since |ξ| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M (unit fact) and θ ≥ 1 on M, H^k(M ∖ spt X) = 0. Consequently, for j ≥ j₀, H^k-almost every x ∈ M at which ω(g_j(x)) ≠ 0 or ω(g(x)) ≠ 0 lies in K″.
 (c) (Integrable dominator.) For j ≥ j₀ put F_j(x) := θ(x)⟨ω(g_j(x)), Dg_j(x)_#ξ(x)⟩ = θ(x)·nVectorPushforward k (fderiv ℝ g_j x) (ξ x) (ω(g_j x)) — the integrand of the statement — and F(x) := θ(x)⟨ω(g(x)), L(x)_#ξ(x)⟩. Using |⟨α, A_#w⟩| ≤ |α|‖A‖^k|w| (Conventions), |ξ| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M, ‖Dg_j‖ ≤ Λ′, ‖L(x)‖ ≤ Λ and (a)–(b): |F_j(x)| ≤ G(x) and |F(x)| ≤ G(x) for H^k-a.e. x ∈ M, where G := ‖ω‖Λ″^kθ1_{K″}. G is H^k⌞M-integrable because K″ is compact and θ is integrable on M ∩ K″ (`integrableOn` of the triple, U = ℝ^D). F_j is H^k⌞M-measurable (g_j is C¹, θ and ξ are measurable), and F is H^k⌞M-measurable: on each chart piece G_i of (e), F∘Φ_i is given by the formula of (f) below in terms of θ∘Φ_i, the measurable coefficient c and the minors of Du (Du is Borel, as an a.e. limit of difference quotients), and Φ_i⁻¹ maps H^k-null sets to L^k-null sets (Φ_i⁻¹ is the restriction of a 1-Lipschitz affine map). Hence F_j (j ≥ j₀) and F are H^k⌞M-integrable.
 (d) (The integrals of the statement.) For j ≥ j₀ the integral in the statement equals ∫_M F_j dH^k by definition (⟨α, w⟩ = w(α); nVectorPushforward k A = A_#), and S(ω) = ∫_M F dH^k. For j < j₀ the integrals play no role (only the tail of the sequence matters for the limit).
 (e) (Chart pieces.) Write M = M₀ ∪ ⋃_{p≥1}M_p (disjoint, H^k-measurable), H^k(M₀) = 0, M_p ⊆ N_p embedded k-dimensional C¹ submanifolds (Simon Ch. 3, Lemma 1.2 and Remark 1.3, which use the C¹ approximation theorem Ch. 2, 1.5; embedded C¹ submanifolds are locally closed, hence Borel). Each point of N_p has a graph chart Φ : Ω → N_p, Ω ⊆ ℝ^k an open ball, Φ(w) = x₀ + O(w, h(w)) with O an orthogonal map and h C¹ with ‖Dh‖ ≤ 1 on Ω; then |DΦ(w)v| ≥ |v|, ‖DΦ‖ ≤ 2 and the Jacobian satisfies JΦ = det(DΦᵀDΦ)^{1/2} ≥ 1. By Lindelöf countably many such charts cover each N_p; disjointifying gives pairwise disjoint H^k-measurable sets G_i (i ∈ ℕ) with M ∖ M₀ = ⋃_iG_i and G_i ⊆ Φ_i(Ω_i) ∩ M_{p(i)}. By (c), F_j and F are H^k⌞M-integrable, so by countable additivity ∫_MF_j dH^k = Σ_ia_i(j) and S(ω) = ∫_MF dH^k = Σ_ia_i, where a_i(j) := ∫_{G_i}F_j dH^k, a_i := ∫_{G_i}F dH^k; and |a_i(j)|, |a_i| ≤ b_i := ∫_{G_i}G dH^k with Σ_ib_i = ∫_MG dH^k < ∞, for all j ≥ j₀.
 (f) (Convergence on one piece: weak continuity of minors.) Fix i; write Φ = Φ_i, Ω = Ω_i, N = N_{p(i)}, u_j := g_j∘Φ (C¹ on Ω, ‖Du_j‖ ≤ 2Λ′) and u := g∘Φ (Lipschitz on Ω; by Rademacher's theorem and the definition of d^Mg via C¹ charts, u is differentiable at Lᵏ-a.e. w ∈ Φ⁻¹(G_i) with Du(w) = d^Mg_{Φ(w)}∘DΦ(w) — only such w are used). Then |u_j − u| ≤ δ_j on Ω. For H^k-a.e. x = Φ(w) ∈ G_i, ξ(x) is a unit simple k-vector orienting T_xM = T_xN = DΦ(w)(ℝ^k) (orientation property of the triple, Ch. 3, Remark 1.5(2) and Remark 1.8(1) together with the Upper Density Theorem Ch. 1, 3.6, which identify the weighted tangent space of (M,θ) with T_xN at H^k-a.e. x ∈ M_p), so ξ(Φ(w)) = c(w)·∂₁Φ(w)∧⋯∧∂_kΦ(w) with c(w) := ⟨ξ(Φ(w)), ∂₁Φ∧⋯∧∂_kΦ⟩/|∂₁Φ∧⋯∧∂_kΦ|² measurable and |c(w)| = 1/JΦ(w) (|∂₁Φ∧⋯∧∂_kΦ| = JΦ). By the chain rule Dg_j(Φ(w))∂_bΦ(w) = ∂_bu_j(w), hence Dg_j(x)_#ξ(x) = c(w)·∂₁u_j(w)∧⋯∧∂_ku_j(w), whose coordinates are the k×k minors M_γ(Du_j(w)) (γ ∈ I(k,D′)); likewise L(x)_#ξ(x) = c(w)·∂₁u(w)∧⋯∧∂_ku(w) at a.e. w. By the area formula for the injective C¹ map Φ (change of variables, Simon Ch. 2, 3.4) and (a)–(b) (which allow inserting 1_{K″}), for j ≥ j₀:
 a_i(j) = Σ_γ∫_Ωψ(w)·ω_γ(u_j(w))·M_γ(Du_j(w)) dw,  a_i = Σ_γ∫_Ωψ(w)·ω_γ(u(w))·M_γ(Du(w)) dw,
 where ω_γ := ω(e_γ) and ψ(w) := 1_{Φ⁻¹(G_i∩K″)}(w)·θ(Φ(w))·c(w)·JΦ(w). Here |ψ| = θ∘Φ·1_{Φ⁻¹(G_i∩K″)}, so ∫_Ω|ψ|dw ≤ ∫_{Φ⁻¹(G_i∩K″)}θ(Φ(w))JΦ(w)dw = ∫_{G_i∩K″}θ dH^k < ∞ (JΦ ≥ 1): ψ ∈ L¹(Ω).
 Weak continuity of minors. Claim: if v_j, v : Ω → ℝ^{D′} are Lipschitz, sup_j‖Dv_j‖_∞ < ∞ and v_j → v uniformly, then every r×r minor M(Dv_j) (rows a₁,…,a_r, columns b₁,…,b_r) converges to M(Dv) weakly-* in L^∞(Ω), i.e. ∫ηM(Dv_j) → ∫ηM(Dv) for every η ∈ L¹(Ω). Proof by induction on r. Since the minors are bounded in L^∞ uniformly in j and C_c^∞(Ω) is dense in L¹(Ω), it suffices to take η = φ ∈ C_c^∞(Ω). r = 1: ∫φ∂_bv_j^a = −∫v_j^a∂_bφ → −∫v^a∂_bφ = ∫φ∂_bv^a. r ≥ 2: let C_q (q = 1,…,r) be the cofactors of the first row, i.e. ± the (r−1)×(r−1) minors with rows a₂,…,a_r and columns {b₁,…,b_r}∖{b_q}. For smooth maps the Piola identity Σ_q∂_{b_q}C_q = 0 holds (the second derivatives cancel in pairs by symmetry), so M(Dv) = Σ_q∂_{b_q}v^{a₁}C_q = Σ_q∂_{b_q}(v^{a₁}C_q); for Lipschitz maps this identity holds in the sense of distributions (mollify v: v^δ → v locally uniformly, Dv^δ → Dv a.e. and boundedly, so all products converge in L¹_loc). Hence ∫φM(Dv_j) = −Σ_q∫v_j^{a₁}C_q(Dv_j)∂_{b_q}φ. Now ∫v_j^{a₁}C_q(Dv_j)∂_{b_q}φ − ∫v^{a₁}C_q(Dv)∂_{b_q}φ = ∫(v_j^{a₁} − v^{a₁})C_q(Dv_j)∂_{b_q}φ + ∫v^{a₁}(C_q(Dv_j) − C_q(Dv))∂_{b_q}φ → 0 (the first term by uniform convergence and the L^∞ bound, the second by the induction hypothesis tested against v^{a₁}∂_{b_q}φ ∈ L¹). So ∫φM(Dv_j) → −Σ_q∫v^{a₁}C_q(Dv)∂_{b_q}φ = ∫φM(Dv).
 Apply this with v_j := u_j, v := u, r = k. Then ∫ψ(ω_γ∘u_j)M_γ(Du_j) − ∫ψ(ω_γ∘u)M_γ(Du) = ∫ψ(ω_γ∘u_j − ω_γ∘u)M_γ(Du_j) + ∫ψ(ω_γ∘u)(M_γ(Du_j) − M_γ(Du)) → 0: the first term is ≤ ‖ψ‖_{L¹}·sup_Ω|ω_γ∘u_j − ω_γ∘u|·k!(2Λ′)^k → 0 (ω_γ is uniformly continuous and |u_j − u| ≤ δ_j → 0), the second → 0 by weak-* convergence tested against ψ·(ω_γ∘u) ∈ L¹(Ω). Hence a_i(j) → a_i as j → ∞.
 (g) (Summation over the pieces.) By (e), (f) and dominated convergence for series (Tannery's theorem: |a_i(j)| ≤ b_i, Σ_ib_i < ∞, a_i(j) → a_i), ∫_MF_j dH^k = Σ_ia_i(j) → Σ_ia_i = S(ω). (For k = 0, nVectorPushforward 0 A is the identity on 0-vectors, F_j(x) = θ(x)ξ(x)(ω(g_j(x))) and F(x) = θ(x)ξ(x)(ω(g(x))), and the convergence is directly dominated convergence: ω is continuous, g_j → g uniformly and |F_j| ≤ G for j ≥ j₀.)
Proof of (II): S̃ = S.
 (II.1) (The push-forward supplied by the premise.) Apply the premise `LipschitzPushforwardIntegerMultiplicity` of the statement, its ambient dimensions and degree instantiated as D, D′ and k, with U := ℝ^D, V := ℝ^{D′} (both open), T := X and f := g. Its hypotheses hold: X is integer multiplicity; g is Lipschitz, hence locally Lipschitz on U; g maps U into V; and for every compact K ⊆ V the set g⁻¹(K) ∩ spt X is compact (properness of g|spt X). It yields an integer multiplicity current S̃ ∈ D_k(ℝ^{D′}) with `IsLipschitzPushforward X g S̃`, i.e. there are M′, θ′, ξ′, L′ such that
  (II.1a) `IsRectifiableTriple univ k M′ θ′ ξ′` (U = ℝ^D): M′ is H^k-measurable and countably k-rectifiable, θ′(x) > 0 for x ∈ M′, θ′ is H^k-integrable on M′ ∩ K for every compact K, ξ′ is H^k⌞M′-measurable, and for H^k-a.e. x ∈ M′, ξ′(x) = ±simpleNVector τ′ for an orthonormal k-frame τ′ spanning a weighted approximate tangent space of (M′,θ′) at x. Nothing more is known about θ′: it is real valued, and it need not be integer valued or ≥ 1;
  (II.1b) X(ω) = ∫_{M′}θ′⟨ω, ξ′⟩dH^k for every ω ∈ D^k(ℝ^D);
  (II.1c) for H^k-a.e. x ∈ M′, every subspace Π with `HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt k M′ θ′ x Π` and every v ∈ Π, the map t ↦ g(x + tv) has derivative L′(x)v at t = 0;
  (II.1d) S̃(ω) = ∫_{M′}θ′⟨ω(g(x)), L′(x)_#ξ′(x)⟩dH^k for every ω ∈ D^k(ℝ^{D′}).
 It suffices to prove S̃(ω) = S(ω) for every test form ω: then, by (I), ∫_MF_j dH^k → S̃(ω) for every admissible sequence (g_j) and every ω, while IsLipschitzPushforward X g S̃ and IsIntegerMultiplicity S̃ hold by (II.1); so S̃ is the current required by the statement. Steps (II.2)–(II.7) compare the two representations (M,θ,ξ) (from `IsIntegerMultiplicity X`) and (M′,θ′,ξ′) (from (II.1a)–(II.1b)) of X; of θ′ only its positivity on M′ and its integrability on compact sets are used.
 (II.2) (Unit orienting k-vectors.) By the unit fact of the Conventions, |ξ| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M and |ξ′| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M′.
 (II.3) (The two vector measures agree on bounded Borel sets.) For γ ∈ I(k,D) and bounded Borel B ⊆ ℝ^D put Ξ^γ(B) := ∫_{B∩M}θξ^γ dH^k and Ξ′^γ(B) := ∫_{B∩M′}θ′ξ′^γ dH^k. These integrals converge absolutely (|ξ^γ| ≤ |ξ| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M and θ is integrable on M ∩ B̄; likewise for θ′, ξ′ by (II.1a)), and for each R > 0, Ξ^γ and Ξ′^γ are finite signed (countably additive) measures on the Borel subsets of the open ball B_R(0). (1) For φ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^D) the form φdx^γ is a test form and ⟨φ(x)dx^γ, ξ(x)⟩ = φ(x)ξ^γ(x), so by the two representations of X (`IsIntegerMultiplicity X` and (II.1b)), ∫φ dΞ^γ = X(φdx^γ) = ∫φ dΞ′^γ. (2) For φ ∈ C_c(ℝ^D) the mollifications φ_ε := ϕ_ε * φ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^D) (0 < ε ≤ 1) converge uniformly to φ, satisfy |φ_ε| ≤ sup|φ| and are supported in the fixed compact set K := {dist(·, spt φ) ≤ 1}; dominated convergence (dominators sup|φ|·θ1_{M∩K} and sup|φ|·θ′1_{M′∩K}) gives ∫φ dΞ^γ = ∫φ dΞ′^γ. (3) For a compact set K_c ⊆ B_R(0) the functions φ_i(x) := max{0, 1 − i·dist(x, K_c)} are continuous with compact supports {dist(·, K_c) ≤ 1/i}, which lie in a fixed compact subset of B_R(0) for i ≥ i₀; 0 ≤ φ_i ≤ 1 and φ_i decreases pointwise to 1_{K_c}, so dominated convergence gives Ξ^γ(K_c) = Ξ′^γ(K_c). (4) The compact subsets of B_R(0) form a π-system generating the Borel σ-algebra of B_R(0) (every open subset of B_R(0) is a countable union of compact sets), and the Borel sets B ⊆ B_R(0) with Ξ^γ(B) = Ξ′^γ(B) form a Dynkin system: it contains B_R(0) (an increasing union of compact sets, by countable additivity) and is closed under relative complements and countable disjoint unions, Ξ^γ and Ξ′^γ being finite signed measures on B_R(0). By Dynkin's π-system theorem, Ξ^γ(B) = Ξ′^γ(B) for every Borel B ⊆ B_R(0), every R > 0 and every γ ∈ I(k,D).
 (II.4) (σ-finiteness of λ := H^k⌞(M ∪ M′), using only θ′ > 0 and the local integrability of θ′.) Let K_q := B̄_q(0) (q = 1, 2, …), compact with ⋃_qK_q = ℝ^D. Since θ is integrable on M ∩ K_q and θ′ is integrable on M′ ∩ K_q (II.1a), θ and θ′ are H^k-measurable on M ∩ K_q and M′ ∩ K_q respectively, and M, M′ are H^k-measurable; so for q, r ≥ 1 the sets
  A_{q,r} := M ∩ K_q ∩ {θ ≥ 1/r},  A′_{q,r} := M′ ∩ K_q ∩ {θ′ ≥ 1/r}
 are H^k-measurable, and by Chebyshev's (Markov's) inequality
  H^k(A′_{q,r}) ≤ r∫_{A′_{q,r}}θ′ dH^k ≤ r∫_{M′∩K_q}θ′ dH^k < ∞,  H^k(A_{q,r}) ≤ r∫_{M∩K_q}θ dH^k < ∞.
 Every x ∈ M ∪ M′ belongs to some A_{q,r} or A′_{q,r}: choose q ≥ |x|, and r ≥ 1/θ(x) if x ∈ M (θ(x) > 0), resp. r ≥ 1/θ′(x) if x ∈ M′ (θ′(x) > 0). Hence M ∪ M′ = ⋃_{q,r}(A_{q,r} ∪ A′_{q,r}) is a countable union of H^k-measurable sets of finite H^k-measure, and λ(ℝ^D ∖ (M ∪ M′)) = 0: λ is σ-finite. (No lower bound θ′ ≥ 1 is used; for the integer valued θ the sets A_{q,1} = M ∩ K_q alone would do.)
 (II.5) (Radon–Nikodym uniqueness.) The vector measures Ξ = (Ξ^γ)_γ and Ξ′ = (Ξ′^γ)_γ of (II.3) are absolutely continuous with respect to λ, with densities κ := θξ1_M and κ′ := θ′ξ′1_{M′}: Ξ^γ(B) = ∫_Bκ^γ dλ and Ξ′^γ(B) = ∫_Bκ′^γ dλ for bounded Borel B. Since λ is σ-finite by (II.4) and H^k is Borel regular (Simon Ch. 1, 2.6), every λ-measurable set is the union of a Borel set and a λ-null set (Simon Ch. 1, 1.12 and 1.15(2), applied to the finite Borel regular measures H^k⌞A_{q,r} and H^k⌞A′_{q,r}, together with λ(ℝ^D ∖ (M ∪ M′)) = 0); hence κ^γ and κ′^γ agree λ-a.e. with Borel functions, and we may assume them Borel.  Consequently θ′(x)⟨ω(g(x)), L′(x)_#ξ′(x)⟩ = θ(x)⟨ω(g(x)), L(x)_#ξ(x)⟩ for every x ∈ Γ, i.e. the integrands of (II.1d) and of S coincide on Γ. subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, 2.6–2.9 and 2.12 (pp. 136–137: representation 2.7 via the Riesz Representation Theorem, Ch. 1, 4.14; characterization 2.8 of μ_T; restriction 2.9; spt T = spt μ_T, 2.12), as summarized in A1 of the parent proof, and A4(b) of the parent proof (restriction of an integer multiplicity current; Ch. 1, 3.6). The steps below supply the details behind those printed statements; the uniqueness argument of Step 7 is the one written in (II.3) of the parent's A3.

Conventions (from the parent proof). I(k,N) is the set of increasing multi-indices γ = (γ₁ < ⋯ < γ_k) in {1,…,N}, e_γ := (e_{γ₁},…,e_{γ_k}), dx^γ := dx^{γ₁}∧⋯∧dx^{γ_k}. For a k-covector α, |α| := (Σ_γ α(e_γ)²)^{1/2} = covectorEuclideanNorm α; for a k-vector w (a linear functional on k-covectors), w^γ := w(dx^γ), |w| := (Σ_γ (w^γ)²)^{1/2}, ⟨α, w⟩ := w(α). Coordinate fact: α = Σ_γ α(e_γ)dx^γ for every k-covector α, hence w(α) = Σ_γ α(e_γ)w^γ and |w(α)| ≤ |α||w|; the map α ↦ (α(e_γ))_γ is a linear isometry of (Λ^k(ℝ^N), |·|) onto ℝ^{I(k,N)}. Unit fact: if τ₁,…,τ_k are orthonormal then |simpleNVector τ| = 1, because its coordinates (simpleNVector τ)^γ = det(τ_i·e_{γ_j}) are the k×k minors of the matrix with columns τ₁,…,τ_k and, by the Cauchy–Binet formula, Σ_γ det(τ_i·e_{γ_j})² = det(τ_i·τ_j) = 1; consequently, whenever IsRectifiableTriple U k M θ ξ holds, |ξ| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M (orientation clause). For a test form ω, ‖ω‖ := sup_x |ω(x)|. H^k = μHE[k]. Fix N, k and X ∈ D_k(ℝ^N) with M(X) < ∞. Degenerate dimensions: if k > N every k-covector on ℝ^N is 0, so every test form and every current of degree k vanish and μHE[k] = 0 on ℝ^N; then μ := 0, v := 0 and Y := 0 satisfy every conclusion (0 is integer multiplicity with M = ∅), and the steps below are also valid verbatim. For k = 0 covectors are scalars (I(0,N) has one element, the empty multi-index), and N = 0 needs no change.

1. Sup-norm bound. If ω is a test form with ‖ω‖ > 0, then ±ω/‖ω‖ is admissible in the definition of M(X) = M_{ℝ^N}(X), so ±X(ω) ≤ M(X)‖ω‖. Thus |X(ω)| ≤ M(X)‖ω‖, and similarly |X(ω)| ≤ M_W(X)‖ω‖ if tsupport ω ⊆ W.

2. Extension to continuous forms. Let C_c denote the continuous compactly supported maps f : ℝ^N → Λ^k(ℝ^N). For f ∈ C_c and a mollifier ϕ_δ, f_δ := ϕ_δ * f is a smooth compactly supported k-form (a test form), ‖f_δ‖ ≤ ‖f‖ (|·| is a norm; Jensen) and f_δ → f uniformly as δ ↓ 0. By Step 1, (X(f_δ)) is Cauchy, so L(f) := lim_{δ↓0} X(f_δ) exists; L is linear, |L(f)| ≤ M(X)‖f‖, and L(ω) = X(ω) for test forms ω (|X(ω_δ) − X(ω)| ≤ M(X)‖ω_δ − ω‖ → 0).

3. Riesz representation (Simon Ch. 1, 4.14 with H := Λ^k(ℝ^N) ≅ ℝ^{I(k,N)}). L satisfies sup{L(f) : |f| ≤ 1, spt f ⊆ K} ≤ M(X) < ∞, so there are a Radon measure μ on ℝ^N and a μ-measurable ν : ℝ^N → ℝ^{I(k,N)} with |ν| = 1 μ-a.e. and L(f) = ∫ Σ_γ f(x)(e_γ)ν^γ(x) dμ(x) for all f ∈ C_c. Let v(x) be the k-vector with v(x)(α) := Σ_γ α(e_γ)ν^γ(x); then v^γ = ν^γ, |v| = |ν| = 1 μ-a.e., and, after changing v on a μ-null set, v is Borel and |v| ≤ 1 everywhere. Thus X(ω) = ∫ v(x)(ω(x)) dμ(x) for every test form ω.

4. Mass of a current with a unit density (2.8). Lemma. Let λ be a finite Borel measure on ℝ^N, u a λ-measurable field of k-vectors with |u| ≤ 1 everywhere and |u| = 1 λ-a.e., A a Borel set, and Y ∈ D_k(ℝ^N) with Y(ω) = ∫_A u(x)(ω(x)) dλ for all test forms ω. Then M_W(Y) = λ(W ∩ A) for every open W ⊆ ℝ^N.
 Proof. (≤) If tsupport ω ⊆ W and |ω| ≤ 1, then Y(ω) ≤ ∫_{A∩W} |ω||u| dλ ≤ λ(A ∩ W). (≥) Let ε > 0. The finite Borel measure λ is inner regular (Simon Ch. 1, 1.15), so there is a compact K ⊆ A ∩ W with λ((A ∩ W) ∖ K) < ε, and by Lusin's theorem (Ch. 1, 1.17) a compact K′ ⊆ K with λ(K ∖ K′) < ε such that u|_{K′} is continuous and |u| = 1 on K′. Let u♭(x) := Σ_γ u^γ(x)dx^γ (continuous on K′, |u♭| = 1 and ⟨u♭, u⟩ = |u|² = 1 there). Extend u♭|_{K′} to a continuous f₀ : ℝ^N → Λ^k (Tietze, coordinatewise), let R(y) := y/max{1,|y|} and choose a continuous χ with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 on K′ and compact support in W; then f := χ·(R∘f₀) ∈ C_c, |f| ≤ 1, spt f ⊆ W, f = u♭ on K′, so ∫_A⟨f, u⟩dλ ≥ λ(K′) − λ((A ∩ W) ∖ K′) ≥ λ(A ∩ W) − 4ε. The mollifications f_δ are test forms with tsupport f_δ ⊆ W for small δ (spt f is a compact subset of the open W), |f_δ| ≤ 1 and f_δ → f uniformly, so by dominated convergence (λ finite) Y(f_δ) → ∫_A⟨f, u⟩dλ. Hence M_W(Y) ≥ λ(A ∩ W) − 4ε for all ε > 0.

5. μ is finite and is the mass measure; the representation. For R > 0 apply Step 4 to λ := μ⌞B_R(0) (finite, since μ is Radon), u := v, A := ℝ^N and the current X — legitimate for test forms supported in B_R(0) — to get M_W(X) = μ(W) for open W ⊆ B_R(0). Since admissible forms have compact support, M_W(X) = sup_R M_{W∩B_R(0)}(X) and μ(W) = sup_R μ(W ∩ B_R(0)), so μ(W) = M_W(X) for every open W; in particular μ(ℝ^N) = M(X) < ∞: μ is a finite Borel measure (IsFiniteMeasure μ). For each test form ω, x ↦ v(x)(ω(x)) is μ-measurable and bounded by ‖ω‖, hence μ-integrable, and its integral is X(ω) (Step 3): IsMeasureRepresentation X μ v.

6. Support (2.12). The zero region Z of X is the union of the open sets W with compact closure on which X vanishes; ℝ^N being second countable, Z is a countable union of such W, and μ(W) = M_W(X) = 0 for each (every admissible form supported in W is annihilated). Hence μ(ℝ^N ∖ spt X) = μ(Z) = 0.

7. Uniqueness of the vector measure (as in (II.3) of the parent). Let (μ′, v′) satisfy IsMeasureRepresentation X μ′ v′.
 (a) Local integrability. If A is bounded Borel and α a k-covector, choose φ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^N) with φ = 1 on the compact set closure(A); ω := φα is a test form and v′(x)(ω(x)) = φ(x)v′(x)(α) is μ′-integrable, so x ↦ v′(x)(α) is μ′-integrable on A. The same holds for (μ, v).
 (b) Fix R > 0 and a covector α. On the Borel subsets B of the open ball B_R(0), Ξ′(B) := ∫_B v′(α)dμ′ and Ξ(B) := ∫_B v(α)dμ are finite signed measures (countable additivity by dominated convergence and (a)). (1) For φ ∈ C_c^∞(B_R(0)): ∫φ dΞ′ = X(φα) = ∫φ dΞ. (2) For φ ∈ C_c(B_R(0)): the mollifications φ_δ ∈ C_c^∞(B_R(0)) (δ small) are supported in a fixed compact subset K of B_R(0), |φ_δ| ≤ ‖φ‖ and φ_δ → φ uniformly; dominated convergence (dominators ‖φ‖·|v′(α)|1_K and ‖φ‖·|v(α)|1_K) gives ∫φdΞ′ = ∫φdΞ. (3) For compact K_c ⊆ B_R(0), φ_i := max{0, 1 − i·dist(·, K_c)} (i large) are continuous, supported in a fixed compact subset of B_R(0), 0 ≤ φ_i ≤ 1, and φ_i ↓ 1_{K_c}; hence Ξ′(K_c) = Ξ(K_c). (4) The compact subsets of B_R(0) form a π-system generating its Borel σ-algebra (open subsets of B_R(0) are countable unions of compact sets), and {B : Ξ′(B) = Ξ(B)} is a Dynkin system (it contains B_R(0), an increasing union of compact sets, and is closed under relative complements and countable disjoint unions). By Dynkin's π–λ theorem Ξ′ = Ξ on all Borel subsets of B_R(0).
 Since every bounded Borel set lies in some B_R(0): for every bounded measurable A and every covector α, ∫_A v′(x)(α)dμ′ = ∫_A v(x)(α)dμ. This is the uniqueness conjunct of the statement.

8. Restrictions (2.9). Let A be Borel and define Y(ω) := ∫_A v(x)(ω(x))dμ. Y is linear; |Y(ω)| ≤ μ(ℝ^N)‖ω‖ since |v| ≤ 1; if ω_j → 0 in the test-form topology then ‖ω_j‖ → 0 (uniform convergence of the 0-th derivatives on a common compact support), so Y(ω_j) → 0. Hence Y ∈ D_k(ℝ^N) (GeometricCurrentOn univ k). With the representation (μ, v) of Step 5, IsRestriction X A Y holds (A is measurable), and Y(ω) = ∫_A v(ω)dμ by definition. subproblem.title: Lemma 5.4: periodic Lipschitz retraction onto the n-skeleton
subproblem.statement: Lemma 5.4 (periodic retraction onto the n-skeleton). Let m, ℓ ∈ ℕ with ℓ ≥ 1, n := m + 1, d := n + ℓ, C := [0,1]^d, q := (1/2,…,1/2). There is c = c(m,ℓ) ∈ [0,∞) such that for every a ∈ ℝ^d with Σ_i(a_i − 1/2)² < 1/16 (i.e. a ∈ B_{1/4}(q)), writing La := L_{ℓ−1}(a) := {y ∈ ℝ^d : there is a set J of m + 2 coordinate indices with y_i − a_i ∈ ℤ for all i ∈ J}, there is a map ψ : ℝ^d → ℝ^d such that (i) ψ(x) ∈ L_n := ⋃_F latticeFace 1 F (the union of the closed n-faces of the unit cubical lattice, F ∈ LatticeFaceIndex (m+1) (m+1+ℓ)) for every x ∉ La; (ii) for every z ∈ ℤ^d and every x ∉ La with z_i ≤ x_i ≤ z_i + 1 for all i, also z_i ≤ ψ(x)_i ≤ z_i + 1 for all i; (iii) for every σ with 0 < σ ≤ 1/4, ψ is Lipschitz with constant c/σ on {x : dist(x, La) ≥ σ}.

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, Lemma 5.4 (p. 160) and its printed proof (displays (1)–(8), pp. 161–163), as reproduced in Part B (B1–B3) of the parent proof. Errata applied: the book's “k” is ℓ (so L_{k−1}(a) is L_{ℓ−1}(a)); the printed bound “|y − a| ≥ 3/4” before (6) is replaced by the correct “|y − a| > 1/4”; the a.e. derivative bound of the printed statement is replaced by the pointwise upper Lipschitz constant |D̄ψ(x)| := limsup_{x′→x}|ψ(x′) − ψ(x)|/|x′ − x| that the printed proof actually estimates in (7)–(8), and Step 6 converts it into the Lipschitz bound (iii) exactly as in the last sentence of B3. Only the properties (i)–(iii) of the statement are proved (they are what the deformation argument uses); the values of ψ on L_{ℓ−1}(a) are irrelevant and ψ := id there.

Notation. n := m + 1 ≥ 1, d := n + ℓ ≥ 2, ℝ^d = Eucl(m+1+ℓ) with coordinates x = (x_1,…,x_d), C := [0,1]^d, q := (1/2,…,1/2). Fix a with Σ_i (a_i − 1/2)² < 1/16, i.e. |a − q| < 1/4; then |a_i − 1/2| < 1/4, so a_i ∈ (1/4, 3/4) for every i. L := L_{ℓ−1}(a) := {y : there is J ⊆ {1,…,d}, |J| = n + 1 = m + 2, with y_i − a_i ∈ ℤ for all i ∈ J} (this is the set La of the statement), d_a(x) := dist(x, L), and L_n := ⋃_{F} latticeFace 1 F (F ∈ LatticeFaceIndex (m+1) (m+1+ℓ)). For a set A ⊆ ℝ^d and a map f defined on A, Lip_A f(x) := limsup_{x′→x, x′∈A} |f(x′) − f(x)|/|x′ − x| (pointwise upper Lipschitz constant at x ∈ A).

1. Elementary facts.
 (a) L is closed (finite union over J of the closed sets {y : y_i − a_i ∈ ℤ ∀ i ∈ J}, each a locally finite union of affine planes), ℤ^d-periodic (y ∈ L ⟺ y + z ∈ L for z ∈ ℤ^d), and a ∈ L. Hence d_a is 1-Lipschitz, ℤ^d-periodic, d_a(x) > 0 for x ∉ L, and d_a(x) ≤ |x − a|.
 (b) x ∈ L_n ⟺ at least ℓ coordinates of x are integers. Indeed latticeFace 1 (z,α) = {x : z_i ≤ x_i ≤ z_i + 1 (i ∈ range α), x_i = z_i (i ∉ range α)} and |range α| = n, so its points have the d − n = ℓ coordinates outside range α integral; conversely, if x_i ∈ ℤ for i in a set I with |I| = ℓ, let α enumerate the complement of I increasingly, z_i := x_i (i ∈ I), z_i := ⌊x_i⌋ (i ∉ I); then x ∈ latticeFace 1 (z, α). In particular L_n is ℤ^d-invariant, and C ∩ L_n = {x ∈ C : at least ℓ coordinates lie in {0,1}} is the union of the n-faces of C.
 (c) Faces of C. For disjoint I₀, I₁ ⊆ {1,…,d} the set F = {x ∈ C : x_i = 0 (i ∈ I₀), x_i = 1 (i ∈ I₁)} is a face of dimension j = d − |I₀ ∪ I₁|, with free coordinates J_F := {1,…,d} ∖ (I₀ ∪ I₁), affine hull Π_F, relative interior {x ∈ F : x_i ∈ (0,1) ∀ i ∈ J_F} and relative boundary ∂F := F ∖ relint F. Every x ∈ C lies in the relative interior of exactly one face (free coordinates = {i : x_i ∈ (0,1)}). Two distinct faces of the same dimension meet in a face of lower dimension, contained in the relative boundary of both. For a j-face F (j ≥ n + 1) let a_F be the orthogonal projection of a onto Π_F: (a_F)_i = a_i (i ∈ J_F), (a_F)_i ∈ {0,1} the fixed value (i ∉ J_F). Since a_i ∈ (1/4,3/4), a_F ∈ relint F, and |y − a_F| > 1/4 for y ∈ ∂F; likewise |y − a| > 1/4 for y ∈ ∂C.
 (d) (Printed (1),(2).) The segment from a to a_F lies in L: its points have the |J_F| ≥ n + 1 coordinates i ∈ J_F equal to a_i. Moreover, for x ∈ F the fixed coordinates x_i ∈ {0,1} (i ∉ J_F) are not in a_i + ℤ, and for i ∈ J_F, x_i ∈ [0,1] lies in a_i + ℤ iff x_i = a_i. Hence L ∩ F = {x ∈ F : #{i ∈ J_F : x_i = a_i} ≥ n + 1}, a finite union of the sets F ∩ {x : x_i = a_i (i ∈ J)}, J ⊆ J_F, |J| = n + 1, each of which is F intersected with an affine plane through a_F. Consequently L ∩ F is a cone with vertex a_F inside F: if x ∈ F ∖ {a_F}, λ > 0 and a_F + λ(x − a_F) ∈ F, then x ∈ L ⟺ a_F + λ(x − a_F) ∈ L.

2. Radial retraction of one face. Let F be a j-face of C, n + 1 ≤ j ≤ d. For v ∈ Π_F − a_F (coordinates v_i, i ∈ J_F, the others 0) let N_F(v) := max_{i∈J_F} max{v_i/(1 − a_i), −v_i/a_i} (the gauge of F − a_F in Π_F − a_F). N_F is positively homogeneous, N_F(v) > 0 for v ≠ 0, F = a_F + {N_F ≤ 1}, ∂F = a_F + {N_F = 1}, and |N_F(v) − N_F(w)| ≤ 4|v − w| because a_i, 1 − a_i > 1/4. Define ψ_F : F ∖ {a_F} → ∂F, ψ_F(x) := a_F + (x − a_F)/N_F(x − a_F): this is the radial retraction of the printed proof (x ∈ {a_F + λ(ψ_F(x) − a_F) : λ ∈ (0,1]}), ψ_F = id on ∂F, and by 1(d), ψ_F(F ∖ L) ⊆ ∂F ∖ L (a_F ∈ L, so F ∖ L ⊆ F ∖ {a_F}).
 Estimate (printed (8)). Let x ∈ F ∖ {a_F}, v := x − a_F, y := ψ_F(x), t := |y − a_F|/|x − a_F| = 1/N_F(v) ≥ 1. For w ∈ Π_F − a_F near v,
 |w/N_F(w) − v/N_F(v)| ≤ |w − v|/N_F(w) + |v|·|N_F(v) − N_F(w)|/(N_F(v)N_F(w)),
 and |v|/N_F(v) = |y − a_F| ≤ diam F ≤ √d, N_F(w) → N_F(v). Hence
 (2.1) Lip_F ψ_F(x) ≤ (1 + 4√d)·t = (1 + 4√d)|ψ_F(x) − a_F|/|x − a_F| ≤ (1 + 4√d)√d/|x − a_F|.

3. The retraction ψ₀ of C ∖ L and the periodic map ψ (printed construction; parent B2). For n + 1 ≤ j ≤ d let ψ^{(j)} be defined on ⋃{F ∖ {a_F} : F a j-face of C} by ψ^{(j)} := ψ_F on F ∖ {a_F}; it is well defined because distinct j-faces meet only in their relative boundaries, where the ψ_F are the identity, and it is continuous (pasting finitely many continuous maps on closed sets agreeing on overlaps). By 2, ψ^{(j)} maps (⋃ j-faces) ∖ L into (⋃ (j−1)-faces) ∖ L. Hence ψ₀ := ψ^{(n+1)} ∘ ψ^{(n+2)} ∘ ⋯ ∘ ψ^{(d)} is defined and continuous on C ∖ L (ψ^{(d)} = ψ_C, a_C = a) and maps C ∖ L into the union of the n-faces of C, i.e. into C ∩ L_n (1(b)). If x lies in the relative interior of a j-face F₁ (j ≥ n + 1), the maps ψ^{(j′)}, j′ > j, fix x (x lies in the relative boundary of every j′-face containing it), so ψ₀(x) = ψ^{(n+1)}∘⋯∘ψ^{(j)}(x), the first map applied being ψ_{F₁}; if j ≤ n then x ∈ C ∩ L_n and ψ₀(x) = x.
 Translation compatibility (printed). Let z ∈ ℤ^d, x ∈ C ∖ L, z + x ∈ C. Let F₁ be the face with x ∈ relint F₁. For i ∈ J_{F₁}, x_i ∈ (0,1) and x_i + z_i ∈ [0,1] force z_i = 0; for i ∉ J_{F₁}, x_i + z_i ∈ {0,1}. So F₂ := z + F₁ is a face of C with the same free coordinates, z + x ∈ relint F₂, a_{F₂} = z + a_{F₁} and N_{F₂} = N_{F₁}; hence ψ_{F₂}(z + x) = z + ψ_{F₁}(x), and ψ_{F₁}(x), z + ψ_{F₁}(x) are again points of C differing by z. Induction on the dimension of the face (the case j ≤ n being trivial) gives ψ₀(z + x) = z + ψ₀(x).
 Therefore ψ(x) := z + ψ₀(x − z) for x ∈ (z + C) ∖ L (z ∈ ℤ^d) and ψ(x) := x for x ∈ L defines a map ψ : ℝ^d → ℝ^d: if x ∈ ((z + C) ∩ (z′ + C)) ∖ L then x − z′ = (z − z′) + (x − z) with x − z, x − z′ ∈ C ∖ L (L is periodic), so z′ + ψ₀(x − z′) = z′ + (z − z′) + ψ₀(x − z) = z + ψ₀(x − z).
 (i) For x ∉ L, choosing z with x ∈ z + C: ψ(x) = z + ψ₀(x − z) ∈ z + (C ∩ L_n) ⊆ L_n (L_n is ℤ^d-invariant). This is conclusion (i).
 (ii) For every z ∈ ℤ^d and x ∉ L with z_i ≤ x_i ≤ z_i + 1 for all i, ψ(x) = z + ψ₀(x − z) ∈ z + C, i.e. z_i ≤ ψ(x)_i ≤ z_i + 1 for all i. This is conclusion (ii). In particular |ψ(x) − x| ≤ diam C = √d for x ∉ L.

4. Claim (3) of the printed proof, pointwise form: there is c₁ = c₁(n, ℓ) such that, for every a with |a − q| < 1/4 and every x ∈ C ∖ L,
 (4.1) Lip_{C∖L} ψ₀(x) ≤ c₁/d_a(x).
 Proof by induction on ℓ ≥ 1 (n fixed), following the printed proof.
 Base ℓ = 1. Then d = n + 1, a point of C with n + 1 = d coordinates in a_i + ℤ equals a, so C ∩ L = {a} and ψ₀ = ψ_C. By (2.1) with t = |ψ_C(x) − a|/|x − a| ≤ √d/|x − a| and 1(a): Lip ψ₀(x) ≤ (1 + 4√d)√d/|x − a| ≤ (1 + 4√d)√d/d_a(x).
 Step ℓ − 1 → ℓ (ℓ ≥ 2). Let x ∈ C ∖ L (so x ≠ a), y := ψ_C(x) ∈ ∂C ∖ L and t := |y − a|/|x − a| ≥ 1; by (2.1), Lip ψ_C(x) ≤ (1 + 4√d)t. Let F be a (d−1)-face of C containing y, say F = C ∩ {x_{i₀} = ε}, ε ∈ {0,1}. The restriction ψ̃_F := ψ^{(n+1)}∘⋯∘ψ^{(d−1)} on F ∖ L is exactly the map ψ₀ of Step 3 built for the (n + (ℓ − 1))-dimensional cube F (coordinates J_F = {1,…,d} ∖ {i₀}) with centre point a_F — for every face G ⊆ F the projection of a_F onto Π_G is a_G — and with dual skeleton L̃ := {w ∈ Π_F : #{i ∈ J_F : w_i − a_i ∈ ℤ} ≥ n + 1}, the set L_{(ℓ−1)−1}(a_F) of the lower-dimensional construction in Π_F ≅ ℝ^{d−1}; moreover |a_F − q_F| ≤ |a − q| < 1/4 for the centre q_F of F, and F ∩ L = F ∩ L̃ by 1(d). By the induction hypothesis (applied in Π_F),

I.5 (M-limits; printed (19)). If (Y_j) are currents in D_k(ℝ^D) with M(Y_j) < ∞ and M(Y_i − Y_j) → 0 as i, j → ∞ (Y_i − Y_j denoting the difference current), then there is Y ∈ D_k(ℝ^D) with M(Y − Y_j) → 0. Indeed |Y_i(ω) − Y_j(ω)| ≤ M(Y_i − Y_j)‖ω‖, so Y(ω) := lim Y_j(ω) exists, is linear, satisfies |Y(ω)| ≤ (sup_j M(Y_j))‖ω‖ (hence is sequentially continuous: ω_i → 0 in the test-form topology implies ‖ω_i‖ → 0), and by lower semicontinuity of mass under weak convergence (2.14) M(Y − Y_j) ≤ liminf_i M(Y_i − Y_j) → 0.  Moreover ∂ψ_#X_ν = ψ_#∂X_ν = ψ_#Z′_ν − ψ_#S_{σ_ν} ⇀ ∂Q, spt ψ_#Z′_ν ⊆ cthickening √d (spt ∂T) and M(ψ_#S_{σ_ν}) → 0; so for every test form ω supported in the open complement of cthickening √d (spt ∂T), ∂Q(ω) = lim(0 − ψ_#S_{σ_ν}(ω)) = 0, i.e. spt ∂Q ⊆ cthickening √d (spt ∂T). By (17)–(19) (mass is continuous under M-convergence):
 (24) M(Q) ≤ cM(T), M(R₁) ≤ cM(T), M(S₁) ≤ cM(∂T);

7. Tangential property (first part of printed (26); parent C7). Let F = (z, α) be a face index, B := ball y r with B ∩ L_n ⊆ latticeFace 1 F ⊆ Π_F, and ω a test n-form with tsupport ω ⊆ B and ω(x)(e_α) = 0 for all x. Otherwise, for every x′ with |x′ − x| < 2ε: x′ ∈ {d_a > σ/2}, so f(x′) = ψ(x′), and |ψ(x′) − f_ε(x)| ≤ |f(x′) − f(x)| + |f(x) − f_ε(x)| ≤ 3Λε < δ₀, so ψ(x′) ∈ B; since x′ ∉ La, ψ(x′) ∈ B ∩ L_n ⊆ Π_F by (S1)(i), i.e. the coordinates ψ(x′)_i, i ∉ range α, equal z_i. Thus f_ε^#ω vanishes on spt X_ν and (f_ε)_#X_ν(ω) = 0 for all small ε, so ψ_#X_ν(ω) = 0. Therefore Q satisfies the tangential property of the statement.

8. Conclusion. Put R := R₁ ∈ D_{m+2}(ℝ^d) and S := S₁ ∈ D_{m+1}(ℝ^d). Source: Simon, Ch. 6, §5, printed “Proof of the Deformation Theorem”, displays (26)–(37) (pp. 167–168), as in C7–C8 of the parent proof, with the tools cited there: Remark 2.35 (with the argument of the Constancy Theorem 2.34), Lemma 2.36 with Remark 2.37(1), Ch. 2, Lemma 2.7, Lemma 2.8 and Remark 2.9, and the lattice-chain facts A7 of the parent. Ch. 2, 2.7–2.9 are applied to the open unit cube Ω = (0,1)^n with centre q, outer radius R = √n/2 and δ = 1/(2√n), so that δ ∈ (0,1) for every n ≥ 1 and the inner ball B_{δR}(q) = B_{1/4}(q) lies at distance 1/4 > 0 from ∂Ω, as the cut-off argument of the printed proof of 2.8 requires; the Poincaré and cut-off estimates are carried out with these parameters in (T4). In the printed proof, display (26) — Q(ω) = Q(ω(e₁,…,e_n)dx¹∧⋯∧dxⁿ) for ω supported in a ball B_y around a point y of an open face F̊ with B_y ∩ L_n = B_y ∩ F̊ — is derived from the construction of Q; here it is the hypothesis (H3) (it is established for the deformed current by the sibling theorem deformation_onto_skeleton), and everything from (27) on is the printed argument. Errata as in the parent: book k = ℓ; supports are stated with “≤ √n”, the parent then passes to the strict bound.

Setting. n := m + 1, d := n + ℓ, ℓ ≥ 1, ℝ^d = Eucl(m+1+ℓ).
Conventions (stated here so that this proof is self-contained). For an ambient dimension D, e₁,…,e_D is the standard basis of ℝ^D, I(k,D) the set of strictly increasing multi-indices γ = (γ₁ < ⋯ < γ_k) in {1,…,D}, e_γ := (e_{γ₁},…,e_{γ_k}) and dx^γ := dx^{γ₁}∧⋯∧dx^{γ_k}. For a k-covector α (`Covector (Eucl D) k`), |α| := (Σ_γ α(e_γ)²)^{1/2} (`covectorEuclideanNorm`); for a k-form ω, ‖ω‖ := sup_x |ω(x)|; for a k-vector w (`NVector (Eucl D) k`, a linear functional on k-covectors), ⟨α, w⟩ := w(α), w^γ := w(dx^γ) and |w| := (Σ_γ (w^γ)²)^{1/2}; ‖A‖ is the operator norm of a linear map A. Coordinate fact: every k-covector satisfies α = Σ_γ α(e_γ)dx^γ (an alternating k-linear map is determined by its values on increasing tuples of basis vectors, and dx^γ(e_δ) = δ_{γδ}); hence w(α) = Σ_γ α(e_γ)w^γ and |w(α)| ≤ |α|·|w| (Cauchy–Schwarz). Push-forward of k-vectors: for a linear map A : ℝ^D → ℝ^{D′}, A_# = Λ_kA := `nVectorPushforward k A` is characterized by ⟨α, A_#w⟩ = ⟨A^#α, w⟩ with A^#α := α(A·,…,A·) (Simon 1.8–1.9); it is linear and A_#(simpleNVector τ) = simpleNVector(Aτ₁,…,Aτ_k) (Simon 1.10; SimonGMT `nVectorPushforward_simple`). Unit fact: if τ₁,…,τ_k ∈ ℝ^D are orthonormal then |simpleNVector τ| = 1, because its coordinates (simpleNVector τ)^γ = det(τ_i·e_{γ_j}) are the k×k minors of the D×k matrix with columns τ₁,…,τ_k and, by the Cauchy–Binet formula, Σ_γ det(τ_i·e_{γ_j})² = det(τ_i·τ_j) = 1; consequently, whenever `IsRectifiableTriple U k M θ ξ` holds, |ξ| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M (orientation clause). Mass M = `mass`, spt = `support`. For a face index F = (z, α) ∈ LatticeFaceIndex (m+1) (m+1+ℓ) write F also for latticeFace 1 F, and let F̊ := {x : z_i < x_i < z_i + 1 (i ∈ range α), x_i = z_i (i ∉ range α)} (relative interior), Π_F := {x : x_i = z_i (i ∉ range α)}, e_α := (e_{α₁},…,e_{α_n}), dx^α := dx^{α₁}∧⋯∧dx^{α_n} (so dx^α(e_α) = 1), Ω := (0,1)^n and ι_F : ℝ^n → Π_F, ι_F(u) := z + Σ_j u_j e_{α_j}, an affine isometry with ι_F(Ω) = F̊ and H^n⌞Π_F = ι_F#L^n. [[F]](ω) := latticeFaceAction 1 F ω = ∫_F ω(x)(e_α)dH^n(x). L_n := ⋃_F F, L_{n−1} := ⋃_F (F ∖ F̊). Hypotheses: (H1) M(Q) + M(∂Q) < ∞; (H2) spt Q ⊆ L_n; (H3) for every F, every ball B = ball y r with B ∩ L_n ⊆ F, and every test n-form ω with tsupport ω ⊆ B and ω(x)(e_α) = 0 for all x, Q(ω) = 0. (H3) is the printed (26) in ball form: by linearity it says Q(ω) = Q(ω(·)(e_α)dx^α) for every test form ω supported in such a ball, i.e. near each point of the open face F̊ the current Q only sees the tangential component of ω, which is the content of p_#(Q⌞F̊) = Q⌞F̊ in (26).

1. Geometry of the skeleton. (a) Every closed n-face of the unit cubical lattice is latticeFace 1 F for exactly one F; a bounded set meets only finitely many faces (local finiteness); hence L_n and L_{n−1} are closed, and a union of any subfamily of faces is closed. (b) The sets F̊ are pairwise disjoint and disjoint from L_{n−1} (two distinct n-faces meet in a common face of dimension < n, which lies in the relative boundaries of both), so L_n = L_{n−1} ⊔ ⨆_F F̊. (c) H^n(L_{n−1}) = 0, and for every γ ∈ I(n,d) the coordinate projection p_γ maps L_{n−1} into a countable union of affine (n−1)-planes of ℝ^n, so L^n(p_γ(L_{n−1})) = 0. (d) For y ∈ F̊ there is r > 0 with B_r(y) ∩ L_n ⊆ F̊: y does not belong to the closed set L_{n−1} ∪ ⋃_{G≠F} G (by (b)), so it has positive distance from it. Let 𝓑_F be the family of open balls B centred in F̊ with B ∩ L_n ⊆ F̊; by (d), F̊ ⊆ ⋃𝓑_F. (e) diam F = √n and M([[F]]) ≤ H^n(F) = 1 (|ω(x)(e_α)| ≤ |ω(x)|).

2. Tools.
 (T1) The sibling theorem deformation_mass_restriction applied to Q and to ∂Q (finite masses by (H1)) gives finite Borel measures μ_Q, μ_∂ with representations (μ_Q, v_Q), (μ_∂, v_∂), μ_Q(ℝ^d ∖ spt Q) = 0, μ_∂(ℝ^d ∖ spt ∂Q) = 0, restrictions Q⌞A, (∂Q)⌞A (Q⌞A(ω) = ∫_A v_Q(ω)dμ_Q) with M_W(Q⌞A) = μ_Q(W ∩ A) for open W, the uniqueness of restrictions and of representing vector measures, and integer multiplicity of Q⌞A when Q is integer multiplicity. In particular μ_Q(W) = M_W(Q), μ_Q(ℝ^d ∖ L_n) = 0 by (H2), and |Q(ω)| ≤ μ_Q(W)‖ω‖ if tsupport ω ⊆ W (same for ∂Q).
 (T2) Lemma 2.36 and Remark 2.37(1) (printed proof): if X ∈ D_n(ℝ^d) has M_W(X), M_W(∂X) < ∞ and E is closed with L^n(p_γ(E)) = 0 for all γ ∈ I(n,d), then X⌞E = 0. [Printed proof: writing ω = Σ_γ ω_γdx^γ, X(ω) = Σ_γ p_γ#(X⌞ω_γ)(dy), dy := dy¹∧⋯∧dyⁿ; for each γ the current p_γ#(X⌞ω_γ) ∈ D_n(ℝ^n) has M(∂p_γ#(X⌞ω_γ)) ≤ M_W(∂X)|ω_γ| + M_W(X)|dω_γ| < ∞ (because ∂(X⌞ω_γ)(ζ) = ∂X(ω_γζ) − X(dω_γ ∧ ζ)), so by 2.35 it is given by a BV function and p_γ#(X⌞ω_γ)⌞p_γ(E) = 0 since L^n(p_γ(E)) = 0; hence M(p_γ#(X⌞ω_γ)) ≤ M_W(X⌞(ℝ^d ∖ p_γ⁻¹p_γ(E)))|ω_γ| ≤ M_W(X⌞(ℝ^d ∖ E))|ω_γ| for spt ω ⊆ W; summing, M_W(X) ≤ cM_W(X⌞(ℝ^d ∖ E)), i.e. μ_X(W ∩ E) ≤ cμ_X(W ∖ E); taking W ↓ K for compact K ⊆ E gives μ_X(K) = 0, and inner regularity gives μ_X(E) = 0.]
 (T3) Remark 2.35 (with the argument of 2.34): if V ⊆ ℝ^n is open and Y ∈ D_n(V) with M_W(Y), M_W(∂Y) < ∞ for open W ⊂⊂ V, then there is θ ∈ BV_loc(V) with Y(g dy) = ∫ gθ dL^n for g ∈ C_c^∞(V), M_W(Y) = ∫_W|θ| and M_W(∂Y) = |Dθ|(W) for open W ⊂⊂ V. [Proof: |Y(g dy)| ≤ M_W(Y)‖g‖, and for g ∈ C_c^∞(W), Y(∂_jg dy) = ∂Y((−1)^{j−1}g dy^{1..ĵ..n}) so |Y(∂_jg dy)| ≤ M_W(∂Y)‖g‖. With θ^{(σ)}(x) := Y(ϕ_σ(x − ·)dy) (ϕ_σ a mollifier), θ^{(σ)} is smooth on V_σ := {dist(·, ∂V) > σ}, ∫_W|θ^{(σ)}| ≤ M_{W_σ}(Y) and ∫_W|Dθ^{(σ)}| ≤ M_{W_σ}(∂Y) for W ⊂⊂ V, W_σ the σ-neighbourhood; by the BV compactness theorem (Ch. 2, 2.6) θ^{(σ_k)} → θ in L¹_loc(V) with θ ∈ BV_loc(V), and Y(g dy) = lim ∫gθ^{(σ_k)} = ∫gθ (ϕ_σ * g → g in C_c^∞). Then M_W(Y) = sup{∫gθ : |g| ≤ 1, spt g ⊆ W} = ∫_W|θ|, and since every (n−1)-form is Σ_j(−1)^{j−1}a_j dy^{1..ĵ..n} with d of it = (div a)dy and |form| = |a|, M_W(∂Y) = sup{∫θ div a : a ∈ C_c^∞(W;ℝ^n), |a| ≤ 1} = |Dθ|(W) (Ch. 2, 2.4; smooth and Lipschitz test fields give the same supremum by mollification).]
 (T4) Ch. 2, Lemma 2.7, Lemma 2.8 and Remark 2.9 for the open unit cube Ω = (0,1)^n, with the parameters R := √n/2 and δ := 1/(2√n). Statement: let q := (1/2,…,1/2) be the centre of Ω, let u ∈ BV(Ω) (u ∈ L¹(Ω) and |Du|(Ω) < ∞, where |Du| is the total variation measure of Ch. 2, 2.2–2.4) and let β ∈ ℝ be a median of u, i.e. L^n{x ∈ Ω : u(x) ≥ β} ≥ 1/2 and L^n{x ∈ Ω : u(x) ≤ β} ≥ 1/2. Then (T4.i) ∫_Ω|u − β| dL^n ≤ c₁|Du|(Ω), and (T4.ii) the function w := (u − β)1_Ω (extended by 0 outside Ω) belongs to BV(ℝ^n) and |Dw|(ℝ^n) ≤ c₂|Du|(Ω), where c₁ = c₁(n) and c₂ = c₂(n) are given below. Proof:
  (a) The hypotheses of 2.7 and 2.8, with a strictly interior inner ball. Ω is bounded, open and convex.    (2) Fix ε with 0 < ε < 1/4 = dist(B_{δR}(q), ∂Ω) (such ε exist because this distance is positive, by (a)), let h_ε : ℝ → [0,1] be a nondecreasing C¹ function with h_ε = 0 on (−∞, ε/2] and h_ε = 1 on [ε, ∞), and put ψ_ε := h_ε∘d_Ω.   (d) Remark 2.9 (combination of 2.7 and 2.8): by (b), ∫_Ω|v| = ∫_Ω|u − β| ≤ c₁|Du|(Ω), and |Dv| = |Du|, so |Dw|(ℝ^n) ≤ (4nc₁ + 2√n + 1)|Du|(Ω); i.e. (T4.ii) holds with c₂ := 4nc₁ + 2√n + 1. In Step 5, (T4) is applied with u := θ_F, and c := max{c₁, c₂} depends only on n.
 (T5) Lattice chains (parent A7). For any β : LatticeFaceIndex (m+1) (m+1+ℓ) → ℝ, P(ω) := Σ_F β_F[[F]](ω) has only finitely many nonzero terms for each test form ω (local finiteness, 1(a)), |P(ω)| ≤ (Σ_{F∩tsupport ω≠∅}|β_F|)‖ω‖, so P is linear and sequentially continuous: P ∈ GeometricCurrentOn univ (m+1); the tsum of a finitely supported family equals its finite sum, so IsLatticeChain 1 β P. 3. Q lives on the open faces (printed (33)). By 1(c), (T2) applies to Q and E := L_{n−1}: Q⌞L_{n−1} = 0, i.e. μ_Q(L_{n−1}) = 0. With μ_Q(ℝ^d ∖ L_n) = 0 and 1(b), μ_Q is concentrated on ⨆_F F̊, and for every test form ω, Q(ω) = ∫ v_Q(ω)dμ_Q = Σ_F (Q⌞F̊)(ω), only the finitely many F meeting tsupport ω contributing; also Σ_F μ_Q(F̊) ≤ μ_Q(ℝ^d) = M(Q).

4. The current on one open face (printed (26)–(28)). Fix F.
 (a) For B ∈ 𝓑_F and a test form ω with tsupport ω ⊆ B: Q(ω) = Q(ω^α), ω^α(x) := ω(x)(e_α)dx^α (a test form supported in B), by (H3) applied to ω − ω^α, whose value on e_α vanishes (ω^α(x)(e_α) = ω(x)(e_α)).
 (b) For B ∈ 𝓑_F and g ∈ C_c^∞(B): Q(g dx^α) = ∫ g·v_Q(dx^α)dμ_Q depends only on g|_{F̊}, because μ_Q(B ∖ F̊) ≤ μ_Q(ℝ^d ∖ L_n) + μ_Q(L_{n−1}) = 0 (B ∩ L_n ⊆ F̊).
 (c) Extensions. For g ∈ C_c^∞(Ω) let ĝ(x) := g(ι_F⁻¹(p_F(x)))χ(x − p_F(x)), where p_F is the orthogonal projection onto Π_F and χ is a smooth function of the normal coordinates with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ(0) = 1, supported in the ball of radius ϱ; for ϱ small the support of ĝ lies in the ϱ-tube around the compact set ι_F(spt g) ⊆ F̊ and inside ⋃𝓑_F (an open set containing F̊). Hence spt P ⊆ ⋃{F : β_F ≠ 0} ⊆ ⋃{F : F ∩ spt Q ≠ ∅} ⊆ {x : dist(x, spt Q) ≤ √n} = cthickening √n (spt Q) (diam F = √n). (b) If F ∩ spt ∂Q = ∅ then μ_∂(F̊) = 0, so |Dθ_F|(Ω) = 0 by 4(e); a BV function with vanishing derivative on the connected open set Ω is a.e. equal to a constant κ (its mollifications have zero gradient), the median of an a.e. constant function is that constant, so β_F = κ and D_F = 0. Hence S = Σ_F D_F vanishes on the open complement of the closed set ⋃{F : F ∩ spt ∂Q ≠ ∅}, so spt S ⊆ cthickening √n (spt ∂Q); and spt ∂P ⊆ spt ∂Q ∪ spt ∂S ⊆ spt ∂Q ∪ spt S ⊆ cthickening √n (spt ∂Q) (∂P = ∂Q − ∂S; a current vanishing on an open set has vanishing boundary there).

8. Integrality. Suppose Q is integer multiplicity. By (T1) (deformation_mass_restriction applied to Q with A := F̊), Q⌞F̊ is integer multiplicity, say Q⌞F̊ = τ(M′, θ′, ξ′) with IsRectifiableTriple univ n M′ θ′ ξ′ and θ′(x) ∈ {1,2,…} for x ∈ M′. Since |ξ′| = 1 H^n-a.e. on M′ (unit fact) and θ′ is integrable on M′ ∩ K for compact K, (H^n⌞M′, θ′ξ′) is a measure representation of Q⌞F̊ (the integrands θ′ξ′(ω) are integrable and integrate to (Q⌞F̊)(ω)); by (27), so is (H^n⌞F̊, (θ_F∘ι_F⁻¹)·simpleNVector e_α). By the uniqueness conjunct of deformation_mass_restriction applied to X := Q⌞F̊ (which has finite mass μ_Q(F̊)), both representations have the same integrals over bounded Borel sets as the canonical one, hence as each other: for every bounded Borel set A and every covector α′, ∫_A θ′ξ′(α′)1_{M′}dH^n = ∫_A (θ_F∘ι_F⁻¹)α′(e_α)1_{F̊}dH^n. Both integrands are integrable on bounded sets with respect to the σ-finite measure λ := H^n⌞(M′ ∪ F̊) (H^n⌞M′ is locally finite because θ′ ≥ 1 is locally integrable), and two such functions with equal integrals over all bounded Borel sets agree λ-a.e. (apply the equality to the sets B_j(0) ∩ {±(difference) > 0}, after replacing the functions by λ-a.e. equal Borel functions). With α′ = dx^γ for every γ ∈ I(n,d) (coordinate fact): θ′ξ′1_{M′} = (θ_F∘ι_F⁻¹)·simpleNVector(e_α)·1_{F̊} λ-a.e. Taking Euclidean norms (|ξ′| = 1 a.e. on M′, |simpleNVector e_α| = 1): θ′1_{M′} = |θ_F∘ι_F⁻¹|1_{F̊} λ-a.e., so |θ_F∘ι_F⁻¹| ∈ ℕ H^n-a.e. on F̊. Hence θ_F is a.e. integer valued and β_F ∈ ℤ by Step 5, for every F; by (T5), P is integer multiplicity.

9. Conclusion. With C := max{2, 1 + c} (c = max{c₁, c₂} = c(n) from (T4) and Step 5), β, P and S satisfy IsLatticeChain 1 β P, Q(ω) − P(ω) = S(ω) for all ω, M(P) ≤ CM(Q), M(∂P) ≤ CM(∂Q), M(S) ≤ CM(∂Q), spt P ⊆ cthickening √n (spt Q), spt ∂P ∪ spt S ⊆ cthickening √n (spt ∂Q), and, if Q is integer multiplicity, β_F ∈ ℤ for all F and P is integer multiplicity. ∎

Near an open face, Q(ω) = Q(ω(e_α)dx^α) (hypothesis = printed (26)) and Q depends only on values on F̊; this defines a top-dimensional current Y_F on (0,1)^n with M(Y_F) ≤ μ_Q(F̊), M(∂Y_F) ≤ μ_∂Q(F̊).
2.35: Y_F = θ_F with θ_F ∈ BV((0,1)^n); identification (27)–(28).

Ch. 2, 2.7–2.9 on Ω = (0,1)^n with centre q, R = √n/2 and δ = 1/(2√n) ∈ (0,1) (δR = 1/4; inner ball B_{1/4}(q) at distance 1/4 > 0 from ∂Ω), ϑ = 1/2: Poincaré inequality ∫_Ω|u − β| ≤ c₁|Du|(Ω) for a median β (convex inner cubes, mollification, smooth Poincaré, mean to median), and the cut-off estimate of the printed proof of 2.8 (cut-offs at levels ε < 1/4) giving |D((u − β)1_Ω)|(ℝ^n) ≤ c₂|Du|(Ω).
Integer-friendly medians β_F of θ_F; with c = max{c₁, c₂}: M(Q⌞F̊ − β_F[[F]]), M(∂(Q⌞F̊ − β_F[[F]])) ≤ cμ_∂Q(F̊) (printed (29)–(32)).
Sum over faces: M(Q − P), M(∂Q − ∂P) ≤ cM(∂Q), |β_F| ≤ 2∫|θ_F|, M(P) ≤ 2M(Q), M(∂P) ≤ (1+c)M(∂Q) (printed (34)–(37)).
Supports within distance √n of spt Q resp. spt ∂Q; integrality of θ_F, β_F and P when Q is integer multiplicity.
